The answer depends entirely on two variables: how much you invest each month and what rate of return you earn. Using a conservative 7% average annual real return (the stock market's historical average adjusted for inflation):

Assumes 7% average annual real return with monthly compounding. Results are in today's dollars.

The most striking column is "Growth" — at every savings level, compound growth does a significant portion of the work. An investor saving $1,000/month reaches $1 million in 26 years, but $688,000 of that is investment growth, not contributions. That is the power of compound interest working over decades in low-cost index funds.

FI community members reach millionaire status faster than the average American millionaire (age 49) for three reasons:

A household earning $100,000 with a 50% savings rate ($50,000/year invested) will reach $1 million in approximately 13-14 years at 7% real returns. That is financial independence by age 40-45 if they start at 28-30. This is not theoretical — thousands of FI community members have documented this exact trajectory.

If you are pursuing financial independence, you are on the millionaire path by design. Here is why:

The standard FI formula is 25x your annual spending. If your household spends $40,000 per year, your FI number is $1,000,000 — you are literally targeting millionaire status. If you spend $60,000, your number is $1.5 million. If you spend $80,000, it is $2 million.

Every FI practitioner is building toward a net worth that exceeds $1 million. The difference between the FI community and the general millionaire population is intentionality: FI community members know their number, track their progress monthly, and optimize their savings rate to get there as quickly as possible.

The data from "The Millionaire Next Door" and subsequent research validates the FI approach completely: live below your means, invest the difference in diversified low-cost funds, avoid debt, and let compound growth do the heavy lifting over 15-25 years. That is the millionaire formula. It is also the FI formula. They are the same thing.

Free calculators, a personalized FI roadmap, and a community of 25K+ on the same journey.

The data says this works. 22 million households have already proven it.

Multiply your annual spending by 25. That is your target net worth. For most FI-minded households, this will be $1-2.5 million — squarely in millionaire territory.

Pro tip: Use your ACTUAL spending, not your income. Spending $50,000/year means you need $1.25 million, regardless of whether you earn $60K or $200K.

The average millionaire lived on 75% of their income during accumulation years. FI community members target 30-60%. Every percentage point increase in savings rate accelerates your timeline.

Set up automatic monthly investments into a total stock market index fund. Max out your 401(k) match first, then Roth IRA, then taxable brokerage. Do not try to pick stocks — even professional fund managers fail at this 90% of the time.

73% of millionaires have never carried a credit card balance. Pay off any existing high-interest debt aggressively, then commit to paying your credit card in full every month. Consumer debt is the single biggest destroyer of wealth-building momentum.

Every millionaire tracked their progress. Calculate your net worth on the first of each month and chart the trend. The visual feedback loop of watching your number grow is the most powerful motivator on the path to seven figures.

If you are saving 20% or more of your income and investing it in index funds, you are following the exact playbook that created 22 million millionaire households. The only question is timing. At a 30% savings rate, you will get there in approximately 22 years. At 50%, approximately 17 years. The formula is proven, the math is clear, and thousands of FI community members have walked this path before you.

There are approximately 22 million millionaire households in the US based on total net worth (assets minus liabilities, including home equity), according to the Federal Reserve Survey of Consumer Finances. If you exclude primary residence equity and count only investable assets, the number is approximately 14-15 million households. Either way, the US has more millionaires than any other country.

Approximately 17% of US households have a net worth of $1 million or more. That is roughly 1 in 6 households. If measuring only investable assets (excluding home equity), approximately 11-12% of households qualify. The percentage has been growing steadily — it was about 7% in 2000.

Overwhelmingly self-made. Chris Hogan's National Study of Millionaires (10,000+ surveyed) found that 79% received zero inheritance. Only 3% received an inheritance over $1 million. The primary wealth-building mechanism was consistent investing in employer-sponsored retirement plans (401(k)s and IRAs) over 25-30 years. The myth that most wealthy people inherited their money is not supported by the data.

The average American millionaire reaches $1 million in net worth at age 49, according to multiple studies. However, this average includes people who started investing late. FI community members who begin saving 30-50% of their income in their 20s frequently reach millionaire status by their late 30s or early 40s — a decade ahead of the average.

Yes, but it requires discipline and time. Saving 20% of a $50,000 salary ($10,000/year or $833/month) invested at 7% real returns would reach $1 million in approximately 30 years. Increasing savings to 30% ($15,000/year) compresses the timeline to approximately 25 years. It is slower than higher earners, but it is mathematically achievable — and many millionaires built their wealth on middle-class incomes.

$1 million supports $40,000/year in spending at a 4% safe withdrawal rate. Add average Social Security benefits ($22,884/year for a retired worker in 2024), and that is about $62,884/year. Whether this is "enough" depends on your location and lifestyle. In a moderate cost-of-living area, it is comfortable. In San Francisco or New York City, it is tight. The FI community recommends calculating YOUR specific number based on YOUR spending — $1 million is a milestone, not necessarily a finish line.

There are 22 million millionaire households in the US — and the data consistently shows they got there through consistent saving and investing, not inheritance, luck, or extraordinary income. The average millionaire earned a solid but not exceptional income, lived below their means, invested in diversified funds for 25-30 years, and avoided consumer debt. If that description sounds familiar, it should — it is the exact blueprint the FI community follows. You do not need to be born wealthy or earn a six-figure salary to join the millionaire club. You need a savings rate above 20%, a low-cost index fund, and enough time for compound growth to do its work. The 22 million millionaires before you have proven it works.

#8985. care validate epm - version 1

Though GLP-1 agonists can be beneficial for weight loss, it’s important to keep in mind that there is limited research on the long-term effects of these medications.

Additionally, research from 2022 suggests that weight regain is likely once you stop taking GLP-1 agonists.

Therefore, it’s best to pair GLP-1 agonists with modifications to your diet and lifestyle. A healthcare professional, such as a doctor or registered dietitian, can also provide ongoing guidance and support to promote long-term weight loss.

GLP-1 agonists are currently approved for three conditions: type 2 diabetes, obesity, and heart disease.

Keep in mind that these medications should be used alongside other lifestyle modifications, including changes to your diet and regular physical activity.

A doctor or other trusted healthcare professional can help determine whether a GLP-1 agonist may be beneficial for you, depending on your health concerns and goals.

Though GLP-1 agonists may support weight loss and help manage blood sugar levels, it’s important to be aware of the possible side effects, such as vomiting, stomach pain, fatigue, constipation or diarrhea, mood changes, and more.

Less common but more severe side effects include:

Because of the risk of side effects, it’s important to check in regularly with a healthcare professional. Additionally, it’s important to discuss any concerns you have about potential side effects with your doctor or other healthcare professional to make sure the medication is right for you.

When you lose a lot of weight quickly, your body loses fat, but it also loses lean mass, including muscle and bone density. This is problematic because muscle is the “engine” of your metabolism, helping you burn energy even when you are resting.

Research shows that people taking GLP-1 medications can lose a significant amount of muscle alongside fat. For example, in studies, about 15% to 40% of the total weight lost was lean mass. Exercise, such as strength training, can help preserve and build muscle while the medication helps you lose fat.

Exercise is also vital for bone health. Rapid weight loss is often linked to a reduction in bone mineral density, which can make bones weaker and more prone to fractures later in life.

A 2024 analysis of a randomized clinical trial found that people using the GLP-1 liraglutide without exercising lost weight but had decreased bone density in the hips and spine. People who combined liraglutide with regular exercise experienced the best weight loss and preserved their bone mineral density.

Exercise also has a lot of other benefits that GLP-1 medications can’t provide, like:

When used along with a balanced diet and exercise, Mounjaro can be an effective off-label treatment for weight loss and long-term weight management. How quickly the drug starts to work and the amount of weight loss can vary between people.

To learn more about what to expect when using Mounjaro for weight loss, talk with your doctor. They can tell you how soon you may see results and help determine what a safe weight-loss goal is for you based on your specific health factors.

#8984. Want to Live Longer? Start Flossing Your Teeth

There’s no shortage of hacks, snacks, and habits that purportedly help you stay healthier for longer. But while we’re busy chasing cutting-edge upgrades—from cold plunges and greens powders to living by the gospel of your Oura ring—we tend to miss out on less sexy yet still powerful tweaks that have been shown to meaningfully move the needle on long-term health.

One such staple is the humble roll of floss, which is probably collecting dust in your medicine cabinet. However, you should probably break it out nightly not just for a brighter, cleaner smile, but to potentially benefit your heart and brain, too.

Keep reading to see why skipping that single strand of string could have consequences that go far beyond tender gums.

If you believe that brushing twice daily will suffice for oral health, you’re in for some sobering news. According to Kami Hoss, DDS, author of If Your Mouth Could Talk: An In-Depth Guide to Oral Health and Its Impact on Your Entire Life, your toothbrush cleans only 60 percent of the surface of your teeth. Read: If you don’t floss, nearly half of your mouth goes uncleaned day after day.

“Flossing is a simple but critical intervention because it disrupts bacterial biofilm between the teeth—areas a toothbrush cannot reach,” adds board-certified periodontist Richard Nejat, DDS. When you floss consistently, you reduce bacterial load, plaque buildup, and gum inflammation—all of which can help keep periodontal disease (a.k.a. gum disease) at bay. And there’s a decent chance you’ll be affected: Per the Cleveland Clinic, about half of adults in the U.S. have some form of gum disease.

The tissue surrounding these small crevices also warrants your full attention. “The sulcus—the shallow groove where your gum meets your tooth—is lined with some of the most permeable tissue in the human body,” Dr. Hoss tells SELF. “It’s richly vascularized, meaning bacteria and whatever compounds we introduce there have a remarkably direct pathway into the bloodstream.” And here’s where the longevity benefits of flossing come into play.

On top of staving off periodontal disease, research shows that regular flossing is associated with reduced risk of dementia, Alzheimer’s disease, and stroke. It can also be an important part of managing diabetes. Meanwhile, poor flossing habits have been associated with a higher risk of cardiovascular disease (CVD) and CVD mortality. And according to one study of over 5,000 older adults, never flossing increased mortality risk by 30% compared to flossing daily.

So how can one tiny string make such a big difference in long-term health outcomes? For starters, you have some unfriendly bacteria to contend with. “Porphyromonas gingivalis, which occurs in the mouth, infects the gums and causes gum disease and periodontitis,” says Jennifer Timmons, MD, a longevity physician and the founder of Timmons Wellness. She says that this bacteria is present in atherosclerotic plaque that can plug arteries during a heart attack, while Dr. Hoss adds that it’s also been found in the brain tissue of Alzheimer’s patients. That’s why addressing it at the source matters. “If you don’t floss, [the bacteria] can enter the bloodstream and lead to blood vessel inflammation, damage, and tiny blood clots that could cause heart attacks or strokes in other areas,” Dr. Timmons warns. (She notes that these are correlations, not proven causations, though the associations are strong.)

Flossing also actively helps decrease inflammation in the gums, thereby preventing a cascade of vascular damage throughout the body, Dr. Timmons explains. After all, inflammation is a major driver of not only gum disease but also the chronic conditions listed above. When you don’t floss, inflammation proliferates in the mouth—and it doesn’t stay put. “Chronic gum disease creates a systemic inflammatory burden that touches almost every major disease category,” Dr. Hoss warns. That doesn’t mean flossing is a panacea, but it highlights how interconnected oral health and overall health really are.

If you already floss daily, rest assured that you’re ahead of the game. For the rest of us who skimp here and there—or have yet to make flossing routine, despite the awkward biannual urges from our dentist—now’s a great time to pick up the habit.

Dr. Hoss advises flossing at night rather than in the morning. “You’re sealing your mouth for six to eight hours. Clearing that biofilm before bed matters far more than doing it after breakfast,” he says. He also recommends good old string floss above the likes of picks and water flossers, as neither can get into the nooks and crannies at and below the gumline as efficiently. (If traditional floss is tough to maneuver, these alternatives are still better than skipping it altogether.) As for the right way to floss? “Curve it into a ‘C’ shape around each tooth and use an up-and-down motion,” he shares.

In short, flossing is crucial to maintain oral health, and good oral health has clear downstream effects on the rest of the body. Since heart disease remains the leading cause of death in the United States—and dementia significantly impacts both quality and length of life —anything that meaningfully reduces risk, even modestly, matters in the longevity conversation. “While flossing alone is not a cure-all for heart or brain health, it is one of the easiest daily habits that can support both oral and overall health,” says Dr. Nejat. All said, flossing might not be revolutionary, but it has surprisingly far-reaching potential.

#8983. What I Learned from Finishing a Triathlon When Everything Goes Wrong

Before the start of her second attempt at the Cowichan Challenge, Anna Rea had high hopes of besting her time from the previous year. (Photo: Courtesy Anna Rea)

For this article, a novice age-group triathlete shared, in her own words, her experience racing the Olympic-distance Cowichan Challenge Triathlon. Despite multiple setbacks, she received encouragement from volunteers and fellow racers to keep going, and has tried to apply that same perseverance to other areas of her life.

It was a perfect early summer morning. The forecast wasn’t too hot, the water was warm, and there was no hint of wind. I had fueled and hydrated the day before. I was well rested and ready. I had done the exact same race one year earlier, which was my first ever triathlon.

This time, I assumed I would be faster. I had to be. Any other outcome would feel like failure.

But within a few minutes of the race start, the rest of the swimmers were barely visible. I had recently done two private lessons with a swimming coach, during which I learned that my technique was broken. There was no time to properly address it before the race.

The swim took 53 minutes, so I was eager to make up some time on the ride. But after five minutes on my bike, just as I was finding my rhythm, my derailleur seized up, and I couldn’t move the pedals. This was defeat.

I tearfully walked my bike back toward transition. I assumed there was no helping this situation. I hadn’t taken my bike for a tune-up before the race. I had failed.

After 25 minutes of walking, a race volunteer spotted me and ran over. He tinkered with my bike for a couple minutes, and I secretly hoped he would confirm my fears – that the bike was broken and it was time to give up. An easy out.

But when he fixed my bike with a couple turns of an Allen key, my guts twisted with dread. He encouraged me to get back on the bike. I told him I had given up, but he told me I might as well keep going since there were still a couple hours until the cut-off time. I had already spent the money, trained, and showed up to the race — I had nothing to lose.

I was alone for most of the ride. I kept apologizing to the volunteers along the race course because I felt guilty that they had to wait for me. I didn’t think I would even start the run, but I kept my focus on the moment, on each corner and hill, until I was back at transition.

My sister, who had completed the sprint distance and was already finished, was waiting for me. I updated her on my situation and asked if she and my mom were OK with waiting until I finished. She said yes and encouraged me.

Then a race worker advised me that the race cut-off was in 52 minutes. He said there was no way I would make it in time and suggested I drop out. I told him I wanted to try, and I accepted that I would complete part of the run without support.

I started the run before I could change my mind. I had a hard time seeing the direction markers on the course. After a couple wrong turns, I was overwhelmed with the urge to give up. I cursed out loud, turned on my heel, and started walking back toward transition. But I immediately met the eyes of an athlete walking back to his vehicle, finisher medal hanging from his neck. He told me to keep going. I told him about my broken bike, the bad swim, not making the cut-off time, and running in the wrong direction. He encouraged me to go anyway, so I did.

I did most of the trail run alone. The race volunteers were supportive and stayed past the cut-off even though they didn’t have to. I was overwhelmed with gratitude, and this time saying thank you was easier than saying sorry.

I shouted curses on the run, stumbling over tree roots in my fatigue, fueled by frustration and determination. When I was 1 kilometer from the end, I almost passed out at a hydration station. I regrouped and kept moving.

Four hours and 15 minutes that felt like an eternity were suddenly coming to an end. I saw the finish line arch. I heard the applause as by now the awards ceremony was well underway. My sister saw me approaching, turned to a group of people behind her, and told them I was coming. And finally, after hours of exhaustion and frustration, wanting to give up the whole time, I crossed the finish line in front of a cheering crowd. And it was all worth it. I wouldn’t change a thing.

I’m not good at this. I don’t feel like I’m good at much. Genetic vision loss has greatly impacted the last few years of my life. I’m struggling to start a new career while managing chronic mental health issues and an acquired disability.

My confidence has taken a hit, and I think about giving up all the time. Things could be a lot worse – I have a support system and free healthcare in Canada. I am privileged with a great quality of life and generally good health aside from my eye disease.

But I feel behind. And by challenging myself to do things like triathlon, I expose myself to people who are incredibly fit. Self-criticism and body dysmorphia usually tag along.

The three months that have passed since that race have been difficult, and I feel out of touch with the person who persevered that day. I’m trying to let some light in and keep going – keep adapting to vision loss, keep building my career, and keep pushing myself.

I used to care a lot more about being good at things. Now I care about following through. Life is hard, and persisting when you don’t feel like enough is a feat of strength. I faced my fear of being slow that day and finished to a crowd of cheers. Of course I want to be faster. I want to finish in the pack. I want to be good at triathlon. But we can learn so much by being bad at things and doing them anyway.

Walking my bike back to the car, finisher medal around my neck, I turned to my sister and said, “Winning is cool, but losing is where it’s at.”

Do things you’re bad at. Challenge yourself. It’s OK if you don’t feel like a triathlete. How many things would you do if you weren’t afraid of failure?

#8981. Single Women Deserve Honeymoons Too—Here’s How to Plan One

I’m on a speedboat whizzing towards my latest vacation destination. As we bounce along, I attempt to take a selfie. The shot I want is the waves, the boats, the islands, but I can’t seem to get the kissing couples out the background. No matter which way I turn, there are honeymooners in my viewfinder. The boat operators and I are the only single people on this vessel. Technically I, too, am a part of a couple—actually, a throuple of single girlfriends heading for an Anguilla getaway. The trip is what I like to call a we-moon.

So often we have our dream destinations on reserve for the day we can go with the person we’ve agreed to spend our life with. There’s the honeymoon and the babymoon, but when do single women get to celebrate life milestones and fulfill the desire for companionship and adventure? That’s the we-moon.

For my most recent we-moon, I was invited to the Four Seasons Resort and Residences Anguilla and joined by two girlfriends. Now, you are probably wondering: What is the difference between this and your average girls trip? Well, similar to a honeymoon or babymoon, a we-moon is taken to celebrate a big life milestone. For me, it was my first book. Single women are so often traveling to celebrate others for their bachelorette or wedding or baby shower. Rarely do we get friends to travel and celebrate something that doesn’t fit into the typical timeline.

That is the purpose of a we-moon. It’s making the phone call to ask your friends to travel and celebrate an achievement with you, just like you do for others. It could be a promotion, a new job, a masters degree, or a book deal.

When crafting the perfect we-moon, there are things to keep in mind to make sure that the trip goes smoothly. I spoke to Joy Harden Bradford, PhD, author of Sisterhood Heals about the best way to pull off a destination celebration with no drama.

“I think having a place where everybody can retreat and have alone time is really good if that is something that the group can do. So private sleeping quarters are important,” she says. “Also having conversations about budget ahead of time. Because some people [might say], ‘Oh, we don't need a five-star hotel. We’re just going to be there to sleep. We’re going to be out.’ And other people are like, ‘No, I like luxury.’ So you don’t want to wait until you get there to find out that there’s a difference in the group about that.”

Another thing you should talk about ahead of time is how many group excursions everyone is down to do. “Because I think for a lot of us, there’s so much going on in our regular life that there’s a lot of expectations for what a vacation should be,” says Dr. Bradford. “‘It’s the one time I get to get away,’ and so people really put a lot on it.”

There are many different vacation styles. We’ve all been on a trip that is overplanned and leaves you more exhausted than when you left. Everyone should discuss what activities they want to do, and a good portion should be optional. For example, we worked on an itinerary with our villa concierge. When it came time to do the private yoga session poolside, some people wanted to rest. So I locked in for a one-on-one session, in which I was able to pay extra attention to modifications and my personal pain points. There were plenty of things that we did together, like an afternoon at the spa, where we all got Anguilla-themed massages, and an excursion across the island in a Jeep to see a different beach. Sometimes you just want to take a nap on vacation, and that is okay.

Me doing yoga with my instructor by the villa pool.

One of the things we did as a group was a margarita-making class. The three of us lined up at the bar of the villa and learned how to properly shake and measure lime juice, orange liqueur, and tequila. Research says that picking up a new skill is good for your brain health. (Although I’m not sure they meant consuming three margaritas in an hour….) The new experience for you can be learning a new sport like pickleball, going to a cooking class, or even playing board games by the beach. This is even better when it becomes a social experiment because even if you fail, you can laugh it off with friends.

What is a girls trip without girl talk? You have to set the mood for conversations. It’s not always a good time to dive deep into your last breakup as you are sitting at a noisy restaurant or relaxing at a spa appointment. But when you are away from your regular routine, there is a great opportunity to open up. “If these are people that you’re actually hoping to grow closer to, then it is important to continue to go deeper with those relationships. And that really requires a lot of vulnerability, which is really hard for people,” says Bradford. “Girls trips really provide a great opportunity and a great backdrop because you are away from your regular routine to maybe get into some of those things that you don’t have time to talk about later.” You have to set the mood for your friends to unravel. For me, I planned a night in the villa's private jacuzzi tub, watching the sunset, and drinking wine. That’s where we shared our work woes and dating troubles as a night cap.

My friends and I having girl talk by the fire.

#8980. 13 Black Women Share How They Found the Strength to Survive—and Thrive—With Breast Cancer

When it comes to Black women’s breast health, the statistics rarely tell a hopeful story. Black women are diagnosed with breast cancer at a younger median age (60, compared with 62 for white women) and are 38% more likely to die from the disease. They have the lowest survival rate for every known stage of breast cancer. And about one in five Black women with breast cancer are diagnosed with hard-to-treat triple-negative breast cancer (TNBC), more than any other racial or ethnic group.

But here’s what the numbers will never capture: the phone calls at 3 a.m., the head-shaving parties, the therapy sessions that cracked something open, the moment a woman looks at her daughter or granddaughter and decides they are reason enough to fight. Black women have always been more than a data point, and perhaps nowhere is that truer than in the way they face, survive, and remake their lives after a breast cancer diagnosis.

The stories below belong to 13 Black women who refused to be reduced to a statistic. They are individuals with careers, children, humor, faith, rage, and joy whose experiences with breast cancer changed them in ways both devastating and profound. In finding their own paths through treatment and beyond, they’ve built something the data can’t quantify: community, purpose, and a hard-won blueprint for survival they’re passing on to every woman who comes after them.

Monique Bass, 53, had always been proactive about her health. A single mother of twin sons and grandmother of four, she started getting annual mammograms at 40. But it was a self-exam at 47 while lying in bed one night that changed everything. She found a lump that didn’t feel right.

What followed were three tissue biopsies of the lump over three years, each coming back benign. Doctors wanted to keep monitoring. Bass pushed back. The lump was growing, and she knew her body well enough to realize something was wrong. She insisted they remove the lump (a procedure called a lumpectomy) and test it. The diagnosis: stage 1 invasive ductal carcinoma that was aggressive enough to require immediate chemotherapy.

Bass got the call while sitting in a car wash. “I felt like I was in The Twilight Zone,” she says. “Not in a million years did I think I would ever hear the words, ‘You have cancer.’” The timing made everything harder. It was 2020, the height of the pandemic, so she navigated much of her journey alone. Adding “another emotional layer,” she was also going through a divorce. Treatment included four rounds of doxorubicin, four rounds of paclitaxel, and 21 radiation treatments. Losing her hair hit the hardest. “But the silver lining is that it grew back even more beautifully after treatment,” Bass says.

Throughout it all her faith anchored her. “I’m not a deeply religious person, but I believe in God, and I knew he had me in the palm of his hand,” Bass says. On the other side of treatment, she founded What’s Behind the Bra?, a New Jersey nonprofit that distributes comfort care packages to breast cancer patients year-round and hosts a weekly podcast of the same name every Sunday at 7:30 p.m. ET.

Jaqueline Beale, 64, comes from a family with a long history of cancer, including her mother, who had breast cancer. That’s why it wasn’t a huge surprise when, at 40, she found a lump during a breast self-exam. Even though a sonogram and mammogram came back clear, it was obvious that something wasn’t right, so Beale got a biopsy.

When the radiologist called with her result—stage 1 breast cancer, which means the cancer hadn’t spread beyond where the abnormal cells had developed—she could hear a lot of noise in the background. He said, “I’m in New York trying to hail a cab, but you have breast cancer. You need to find a breast surgeon.” Despite the bluntness, Beale says she couldn’t help but find the humor in the situation, which is something she carried with her through treatment.

“I made sure that I surrounded myself with laughter and love,” she says, “and I told my family that I knew they loved me, but I also needed a lot of laughter to get through it.”

She recalls one incident in an elevator after her sister had taken her to a chemo treatment. “I had been sick as a dog after, and a woman got in and asked if I was okay. My sister said, ‘Oh, she’s fine. She’s just got a little bit of cancer.’ The woman looked horrified, but I laughed. My family knew that their sense of humor is what I needed.”

Annita White, 51, was five months late for her mammogram. As a single mother of two boys, a higher education administrator, and a first-year PhD student, she always had something more pressing. When she finally went, she expected the usual letter in the mail saying everything was fine. Instead, she got a call. There was a mass that hadn’t been there before.

By the time the biopsy came back, she already knew. A technician had commented on how hard the mass was, and White felt the diagnosis in her spirit before the words were ever spoken. The confirmation came the next day. “When I got the call, I fell to the floor and cried tears of desperation,” she says. “My first thought was, ‘Lord, I can’t do this.’”

What followed was hard in every way: chemotherapy, losing her breasts, losing her hair, which had always been full. “Being bald left me feeling vulnerable and insecure,” White says. “Physically, losing my breasts and going through chemotherapy made me feel like my body was no longer my own.” Through it all the fear that drove her was running out of time—time to see her sons become men and to meet her grandchildren someday.

Her faith, which she’d been privately wrestling with for years, met her exactly where she was. She’d been asking God to truly show up in her life. “He did,” she says. “In the middle of one of the hardest seasons of my life, he carried me through.”

Three years later White is cancer-free, her hair is back, and she recently finished her PhD. She now walks in her purpose as Dr. Nita, a member of the African American Breast Cancer Alliance survivor network, sharing her story and those of others facing the disease. “What once felt like the end became the beginning of something greater,” she says.

Marylande Regis, 38, had been in her new Georgia home for four months when everything changed. A registered nurse, realtor, wife, and mother of three, she had just stopped breastfeeding her nine-month-old when she found the lump. Her baby had never latched well on that side. When she messaged her provider, the on-call response was that it was probably a clogged milk duct and that she was too young to worry about it being something more serious. Regis didn’t accept that. She called back and left a message, insisting that something was wrong. “Another ob-gyn saw the message and encouraged me to make an office appointment immediately,” she says. Within two weeks she had a diagnosis: aggressive stage 2B, BRCA1-positive breast cancer. Within two more weeks what had been one tumor and one impacted lymph node had become three tumors and four impacted lymph nodes. Regis was 36.

“I was relieved that I advocated for myself,” she says. “I was proud that fear didn’t factor into my decision.”

What followed was relentless. Regis went through six months of chemotherapy, a bilateral mastectomy, six weeks of radiation, a total hysterectomy (to eliminate her body’s main source of estrogen), and breast reconstruction, all over a span of roughly 18 months. She lost friends to cancer along the way, as well as a cousin diagnosed around the same time. Her faith was, as Regis describes it, “shaken and stirred and flipped every way possible.” She wrote the important letters. She wrote her own obituary. She was practical about it. “I wanted to be positive, but I am also very realistic,” Regis says.

The hardest part wasn’t any single treatment—it was losing control. As her family’s go-to planner for everything from doctor’s appointments to vacations, she found it foreign to ask for help. But when she told her parents, her mother showed up and never left. “We joke, but my mom never went home,” Regis says. “This is her house now.” Her husband, Kory, came to every appointment and held steady even through both of them losing their jobs. “He deserves a trophy,” she says.

As the daughter of Haitian immigrants, raised to be everything her parents couldn’t be, Regis says the fight was never just medical. Today strength looks different than it did before cancer. It looks like making it to the bus stop with her son, who has autism. It looks like seeing her oldest finish nursing school and work toward becoming an ob-gyn. It looks like watching her youngest hit milestones like learning to talk. “I would have missed that if I didn’t fight,” she says. “The clouds are moving. The sun has decided to show itself. I can’t wait to soak it all in.”

Illness had always been an afterthought for 75-year-old Judy Fambrough-Billingsley. Why would it cross her mind? She walked three miles every day, swam laps all summer, took Zumba classes, and played soccer for 30 years. Judy Fambrough-Billingsley had never smoked or drank, and she didn’t even need to take medication. Being healthy wasn’t something she worked at; it was just who she was. A naturalized American citizen born in Germany, she traveled back to her home country regularly to visit family. Her life was full and active.

So when she felt a lump—and then another six months later—she ignored them. After all, she’d had a clean mammogram earlier that year. But when she noticed them growing and multiplying, she went back to her doctor. The results were not what she expected.

“I was shocked,” Fambrough-Billingsley says. She suddenly found herself navigating an entirely new set of experiences: prescription bottles, hospital procedures, lab processes—the whole medical system. “Being a part of a world where sickness exists had never been my world until now,” she says.

What carried her through was far older than her diagnosis. She grew up during the Civil Rights Era, the daughter of a successful Black entrepreneur who built his business during tumultuous years in US history. Both her parents were lifetime members of the National Association for the Advancement of Colored People (NAACP). She was president of the NAACP Youth Council and an active member of the Student Nonviolent Coordinating Committee. Fambrough-Billingsley knows something about fighting for your life in systems that weren’t built for you.

“Growing up during the Civil Rights Era contributed to this era of fighting,” she says. “Never giving up.” That same spirit—the one her parents modeled, the one she fell into during her work as a community organizer and across decades of a life fully lived—is the one she’s bringing to this too. She may still be on her breast cancer journey, but this is not her first fight.

Taylor Johnson was nearly 30 when she found the lump on her left breast. A mom and content creator who loves trying new things and staying active, she went to her primary care doctor, who referred her for an ultrasound and a mammogram. Johnson was denied a mammogram—she was told she was too young. She pushed anyway, got a biopsy (in lieu of the mammogram), and days later, had a diagnosis: stage 2 triple-negative breast cancer.

“My reaction was a very deep pause, trying to process what my doctor had told me,” Johnson says. “It then hit me, and all I could do was cry.”

She’s in the middle of her treatment plan, which includes six months of chemotherapy, followed by surgery and three weeks of radiation. After finishing chemo Johnson felt confident that would be the hardest part of her journey, both physically and emotionally. But her own health wasn’t her only concern: She knew her five-year-old was watching her every move, and she wanted to stay stable for her daughter. “I was so used to always being the strong one,” Johnson says. “This definitely tested that.” She held it together not because it came easily, but because she understood what her daughter was absorbing.

She is grateful for the community that rallied around her while she waited. Weekly prayer calls, rotating visits from family and friends, and a medical team at Mayo Clinic in Arizona that went above and beyond carried her through.

Though Johnson hasn’t finished treatment yet, completing chemo clarified something for her. “It has reassured me how strong I truly am,” she says. Strength, she’s learned, isn’t just physical. The emotional and mental muscle it takes to keep going counts just as much.

Jessica Ncube, 41, built her life around caring for others. A licensed clinical social worker, the co-owner of a mental health practice, and a mom, she was always in motion. Her life revolved around showing up for others and helping them navigate their hardest moments. “Looking back I do not know that I was always receiving,” she says.

Her diagnosis came quietly. A routine mammogram caught it; nothing in her body had felt amiss. That silence, Ncube says, is exactly why early detection matters. When she got the news she went into survival mode. “You hear the words, but it takes time for them to land,” she says.

Ncube’s journey started with a lumpectomy. When her margins came back unclear, meaning the pathologist could not determine whether all the cancerous cells were removed, she made the decision to move forward with a double mastectomy with reconstructive surgery. “Losing a part of your body, even when it is lifesaving, is still a loss,” she says. “The hardest part was learning how to sit in both gratitude and grief at the same time.”

As someone professionally wired to be strong for others, letting that tendency go was its own kind of work. “Strength became less about holding everything in and more about being honest about what I needed,” Ncube says. Her faith grounded her, and her community showed up, but she also had to unlearn something deeply familiar. “As a Black woman there is a resilience that is almost ingrained in us,” she says. “I had to learn how to balance that resilience with softness.”

After completing treatment Ncube has become more present and deliberate. Her definition of strength has changed entirely. “Strength today is softness. It is honesty. It is allowing myself to receive, to rest, and to not have all the answers,” she says.

Ameiko Newman, 40, didn’t learn of her diagnosis through a routine screening. She was rushed to the hospital for abdominal pain, and that’s when she learned she had breast cancer. Life before her diagnosis had been stressful, uncertain, a season of not quite knowing where she was headed. In a strange way, cancer gave her direction.

“For me, cancer saved me,” she says. “It made me a better person. It made me fight harder, push through the hard times and know what I want in life.”

Newman is still in treatment, receiving chemotherapy and immunotherapy every week, and she is honest about what that looks like: There are good days and bad days. She goes to church faithfully, prays every day, and tries to stay positive through it all.

What has surprised her most is that in the middle of fighting for her own life, she found her purpose: helping others fight for theirs. Newman rebranded her business entirely around that mission and started designing scarves with chemo patients in mind. “I started making them mainly for my Black women because you know we love having style,” she says. But a wide variety of women from all over have since bought them.

She wakes up every day, gets her kids ready, works out, and moves through life. Faith, she says, is what makes that possible. Her message to any Black woman who’s just gotten diagnosed is both simple and hard-won: “Cancer doesn’t define you. You define you. Even though you’re fighting for your life, help someone else fight for theirs.”

Charlotte Connor, 38, had just undergone a breast augmentation when she felt a lump in her breast. “When I saw my doctor, they weren’t concerned, in part because of my young age,” says Connor, who was 30 years old at the time. She had a mammogram and ultrasound to check for signs of cancer, but no MRI. “Looking back now I wish I would have asked for that MRI,” she says.

At the first checkup six months later, they told her she was fine. At the second—one year after the original lump was found—the lump had tripled in size. Her doctor ordered a biopsy, and her diagnosis was confirmed: stage 2A ductal carcinoma, which means the cancer was growing but contained to the breast and surrounding lymph nodes.

“When they told me I had cancer, I was calm,” she says. Her mindset immediately shifted from a sinking feeling to being optimistic about the future. “I focused on getting healthy again,” says Connor, who started fantasizing about what she would do after treatment.

She remembers thinking, I may be feeling sick and throwing up from chemotherapy, but what restaurants am I going to go to after all this is over? It’s an outlook that didn’t necessarily come naturally to her, either. “I’m not even overly optimistic in life—I think I’m a realist—but in this situation, I shifted to being overly optimistic.”

Part of that mindset shift was for her young daughter. “I couldn’t be pessimistic; I had to be strong for her,” she says. “And I knew that how I acted in this situation was how she was going to mirror things and react to stressful situations when she got older.”

Connor’s other pillar of support came from a tight-knit circle of friends and family, who threw her a head-shaving party before she lost her hair due to chemo. “Making things fun and lighthearted like that got me through my darkest, saddest moments,” she says.

It was 1999, and Donna Culmer had just received a clean mammogram. A few months later she felt a stone-size bump on her right side, so she went back to her ob-gyn to get it checked out. They redid the mammogram on both breasts, and while what she’d felt was actually a fibrocystic lump, the imaging found a small, not palpable spot on her left side that turned out to be a stage 1 cancer. “I was stunned,” Culmer says. “I didn’t even know what questions to ask.” She drove back to work in a daze and told her boss what had happened.

At 46 she was serving in the Navy as an instructor and trainer to personnel who were working alongside the Marines. She was married to a Marine and raising three children. There was no good moment for this. There never is.

Four months of chemotherapy followed, with nausea and exhaustion that never quite let up. Her doctors were concerned that the chemo might not work, so she had a mastectomy. Through it all her community refused to let her go through it alone. Her father drove her to every session and sat with her. Her church came to her, literally; services were held at her house.

Twenty-seven years later, Culmer, now 73, has had time to reflect. “As Black women, we have been through challenges our whole lives,” she says. “This is just one more.” Her advice is practical and clear. “Don’t panic and ask questions, even if you have to write them down,” Culmer says. “The treatments available now are so much better than what I had.”

One morning, Patricia Fox, 38, woke up with a lump in her right breast that wasn’t there the night before—she was just 26 years old at the time. Fox scheduled an appointment with her ob-gyn that day. “They told me that I was a young Black woman and had dense breasts, and it was likely a cyst,” she says. “They were ready to turn me away.”

The lump, which was a little smaller than a golf ball, seemed strange to Fox. Thankfully, she listened to her intuition. “There was something telling me to get it checked out,” she says, so her doctor did a biopsy just to be sure.

Her results came back as estrogen receptor-positive stage 2A breast cancer, meaning her cancer had estrogen receptors that would respond to hormone therapy drugs. Fox says she’ll never forget her doctor’s words: “Patricia, you’ll be a breast cancer survivor.” That sentiment set the tone for her mindset as a fighter. “It made me think that I could face this and survive this,” she says.

Still, cancer treatments quickly overwhelmed Fox, and soon she faced her lowest point: crying on the floor for hours, feeling like having cancer at such a young age was a punishment for being a “bad person.” But she pulled herself out of it with hard work in therapy.

“I found that talking to a therapist helped me process my diagnosis and examine the areas of my life—certain people and my own behavior patterns—that were cancerous for me that I needed to do something about,” she says. “While therapy didn’t make the pain go away, it did make how I coped with it much better.”

In the Black community, therapy is often taboo, says Fox, but it’s become her mission to dispel that belief. “Therapy fortified me to get through cancer,” she says, “and I tell everyone that they don’t have to suffer in silence.”

Annette Colden, 63, was sitting at her sister’s bedside during the last days of her final battle with breast cancer when the conversation turned to screenings. Her sister had been through cervical cancer and two bouts of breast cancer before passing away from the disease. “She made me promise I’d get my mammograms,” Colden says.

Colden’s first two yearly mammograms were clear. On the third there was a spot, but she was told by her doctor that things looked okay and it wasn’t cancer—she just had lumpy breasts.

“There’s this inner feeling you have,” she says. “Something was inside me saying, That’s not right.” Her sister’s doctor had told her the exact same thing, but Colden was so happy to hear she didn’t have cancer that she didn’t follow up.

A year later she went back for a mammogram, and that’s when her doctors found it: stage 0 breast cancer, meaning only abnormal cells had been found. She was 42. “Now, looking back, I always tell women that if something doesn’t feel right, get a second opinion.”

Despite the diagnosis Colden remained calm. “I’m a religious person,” she says. “In my prayer I said, ‘Lord, if you will be my pilot on this journey, I’ll be your copilot.’” She immediately felt a sense of peace.

After her recovery she decided to share that calming presence with other women going through breast cancer at a support group through Roswell Park Comprehensive Cancer Center, where she had treatment. “I say, ‘It’s going to be a long road. If you don’t want to travel it alone, I’m right there with you.’”

And she means it. Sometimes that involves talking with someone at 3 a.m. when the pain from chemotherapy hits. Other times it means sending food delivery boxes to the homes of people with breast cancer who can’t muster the strength to leave. “My sister did a lot of support work before she got really sick,” she says. “This is her vision.”

Ricki Fairley, 69, was in the security line at the airport for a work trip when she got a call from her doctor. They’d found a peanut-like lump under her nipple that turned out to be cancer.

Fairley, who was 55 at the time, said, “I don’t have time for this right now. I’ll call you when I get to my destination.” A couple days later she found out she had stage 3A TNBC, and it was really aggressive. Compared with other breast cancers, TNBC has fewer targeted-therapy treatment options, often spreads beyond the breasts, and is more likely to recur. Black women have nearly three times the risk of developing triple-negative breast cancer.

Her diagnosis woke her up. “It made me realize that I needed to get all of the ‘cancers’ out of my life,” Fairley says. During treatment that first year which involved a double mastectomy, aggressive chemotherapy, and radiation, she quit her job and started her own company. Then she filed for divorce and later sold her house. “I quit my life and started a new one, and changed everything,” she says. “I had to learn that my peace is nonnegotiable. I really think that stress caused my breast cancer.”

A year later her life changed again. Fairley was diagnosed with metastatic breast cancer and told she had two years to live. After finding out her current doctor had only treated two previous cases of TNBC and both women had died in eight months, she found a new doctor, who was well-versed in current research and treatments for the disease. She beat cancer a second time. “I remember sitting at my daughter’s graduation thinking, Okay, I made it. What’s next for me?” Fairley says. The answer: helping others. In the years that followed, Fairley cofounded The Black Breast Cancer Alliance, which works to reduce the mortality rate for Black women.

#8979. Infographic | The Cost of Health “Optimization”

If you’re like most people, your answer is probably, “Yes!”

And, you probably want to live not only a longer life, but also a healthier one.

If so, you don’t have to look very far to find claims about how to improve—no, “optimize”—your health.

Want to reverse chronic disease? Extend that youthful glow? Live to 115… or forever? Lots of fitness influencers, authors, and podcasters will tell you how to do it.

But are their ultra-specific, advanced protocols necessary—or even effective?

And just how much effort, time, and money do these methods really require?

Most of all: Are the benefits worth the trade-offs?

By the end of it, you’ll have clarity about how to get the health and longevity you want, while living a life you enjoy.

Click here for a fully printable version of this infographic.

#8978. The Best Triathlon GPS Smartwatches of 2026

If you buy through our links, we may earn an affiliate commission. This supports our mission to get more people active and outside.Learn about Outside Online's affiliate link policy

How we reported this: Editor-in-chief Chris Foster has spent hundreds of hours using these watches for training, everyday wear, and nighttime metrics. Foster has independently tested nearly every smartwatch/GPS watch that’s been released in the last eight years, and draws on a decade of making a living as a pro triathlete to inform his impressions. The brands provide all watches on loan.

If you’re a triathlete in the market for a smartwatch or GPS watch, the options just keep getting better. Some of the best triathlon watches in 2026 are getting cheaper, and high-end features that used to cost over $800 are coming down into the $400 range.

What is the only differentiator between a good GPS watch for triathletes and a great one in 2026? It boils down to which is easiest to use, which has those sneaky features you didn’t know you needed, and what you’re (actually) going to do with it.

Below we’ve got brand-new, editor-tested smartwatches and GPS watches from Suunto, Apple, Coros, Amazfit, and Garmin that have all been released in fall 2026. Our editors spend hours training and sleeping with these watches to see what works as advertised, what provides the most accurate (and useful) information, and if it’s intuitive or not.

We review these through the lens of a triathlete who trains multiple times per week, wants to know how their body is reacting to their training, and relies on the data and information for important training and racing decisions. Read on for our expert impressions.

We’ve also included a “Where does it stand?” section for each watch to help you understand where it fits in today’s smartwatch universe. And if you want to dig deeper, we’ve got links to longer reviews for most of the watches below.

Looking for an older smartwatch? We don’t miss much, so check out our previous roundups for quick looks and deep dives on watches from previous years, like the Garmin Fenix 8 or the Suunto Race S – take a look at the 2024 roundup for more.

We’ve also got watches from 2023, like the Polar Pacer, Coros Apex 2 Pro, Garmin Forerunner 965, Suunto 9 Peak Pro, Apple Watch Ultra 1, and Garmin Enduro 2. Or watches from 2022, like the Timex R300, Wahoo Rival, Apple Watch Series 7, Garmin Instinct 2 Solar, Polar Grit X Pro, Suunto 9 Peak, Coros Vertix 2, and Garmin Fenix 7X Solar. Or our 2020 buyer’s guide with reviews of the Coros Pace 2, Apple Watch SE, Garmin Forerunner 745, Fitbit Sense, Polar Vantage V2, and Suunto 7.

The Suunto Race 3S is the little cousin of a slightly larger (but cheaper) Race 2. The Race 3S has a 1.32-inch AMOLED touchscreen that maxes out at 2,000 nits, with 45 hours of multi-band GPS and 64GB of offline mapping and music storage. Like the Race 2, it has sapphire crystal glass, but unlike the Race 2, it weighs in at around 56g compared to the Race 2’s beefy 76g.

The specs are pretty much what you’d expect for a watch in the $400-600 price range, and in real-life testing, the Race 3S also felt nearly identical to the brand-new $400 Suunto Run 2, which was just released about a month ago: They look nearly the same, they feel, weigh, and perform pretty much exactly the same, but the Run 2 only has 24 hours of multi-band GPS and 10 days of advertised daily use (though we found less than that, closer to right days). That said, the Run 2 is $200 cheaper than the Race 3S, so you’re basically paying $200 for a little more battery life, but materially not much else.

While the Race 3S is a fine smartwatch out of context, once you put it up against other smartwatches in the $400-600 range, it struggles a little bit to find its place. First, the elephant in the room is that the Suunto Race 2 has more battery life (and a bigger screen, for better or for worse) for less money. In some ways, the Race 3S is more like a Race 2S, especially given that it’s almost unfair to compare the Race 3S to the original Race S that was released two years ago. But even then, if this was a Race 2S (which it’s not), you’d really have to want a slightly smaller watch to spend less money on an arguably better watch in the Race 2.

The next problem for the Race 3S is also competition from the $400 Run 2, which still isn’t my favorite watch of the year, simply because of the biggest issue Suunto has here: the presence of the $450 Coros Pace 4 Pro. The Pace 4 Pro costs (way) less than the Race 3S, has a bigger screen, weighs slightly less, and has about the same battery life.

The other competition in this price range – watches like the Garmin Forerunner 570 ($550) or the $500 Polar Vantage M3 don’t really overpower the Race 3S, but they’re also not obviously a worse choice. That said, if you put the Race 3S up against Suunto’s own $600 Vertical 2 – with much more battery life, a bigger screen, and an awesome LED flashlight, it’s not even a fair fight. I’d easily spend another $100 for that watch, but it’s the same price.

That said, I’m not sure exactly who the Suunto Race 3S is for. It faces stiff competition from older Suunto watches, like the Race 2 or the Vertical 2, and it struggles mightily against watches like the Coros Pace 4 Pro, or even the $250 Coros Pace 4 (if size/weight truly is your goal and you really need a smaller, ultra-lightweight watch with just enough features and onboard mapping).

The Coros Pace 4 Pro is the latest in one of my favorite lines of endurance-focused smartwatches. Beginning with the almost-too-cheap Pace 2, Coros has taken chunks out of the smartwatch market with a super lightweight and entirely capable offering that doesn’t break the bank. Released less than a year ago, the Pace 4 was arguably one of the best smartwatches for the money, and it was hard to imagine what could come next.

But here we are with the Pace 4 Pro, boasting a big, bright 37.3mm screen with a blinding 3,500nits. This is a big deal because in bright sunlight, if you’re actually using the 32GB of onboard navigation, you need a big screen to see it all, and it needs to be bright enough to see in direct sunlight. Pair those features with the digital dial (essential for zooming navigation on the go, in my opinion), and you’ve already got a best-in-class watch for routing and mapping. All for $450.

Past that, at 51g plus a super-thin side profile, the Pace 4 Pro disappears on one’s wrist in a way that very few watches with these features do. For those of us with small wrists (or those of us who struggle to remove a wetsuit quickly over their watch), this is a big deal.

If there’s room to complain, the only caveat with the Pace 4 Pro is that the styling is still extremely sporty, and the design doesn’t really lend itself to all-day wear. The titanium case and sapphire glass do help with durability, but I still maintain that the aesthetic isn’t quite there on the mid-to-lower end of the Coros line.

All in all, the Coros Pace 4 Pro is a strong contender for the best watch of the year, especially in the highly competitive $400-600 price range (more on that below), and you’d have a hard time feeling limited with this watch.

First it’s worth noting that the $400-600 price range is by far the most competitive in sport-focused smartwatches. For $450 you can get pretty much everything you used to find on a $1,000 watch — and in many cases these less-expensive models are better than the top of the pile just a few years ago.

The $450 Coros Pace 4 Pro most squarely competes with the Garmin Forerunner 570 ($550), the Polar Vantage M3 ($500), the Coros Apex 2 ($480), the Suunto Race 2 ($500), and the Suunto Vertical 2 ($600). You could also include the new Suunto Run 2 ($350), but I don’t think that’s a fair fight.

To my mind, only the Suunto Race 2 and the Suunto Vertical 2 truly compete because the Forerunner 570 costs more and has way less battery (and a smaller screen), the Polar has a host of issues, and the Apex 2’s screen isn’t even in the same league as the Pace 4 Pro.

When squared up against the Suunto Race 2, you’re spending $50 more for a watch with slightly worse battery life, a similarly sized screen (though not as bright as the Pace 4 Pro), but arguably better styling. The Race 2 is also heavier (by a bit) and bulkier.

When up against the Vertical 2, the Suunto easily wins on battery life and the not-to-be-ignored LED flashlight (early morning transitions anyone?) with a similarly sized screen, but it’s a chunker to be sure and costs $100 more — it also lacks a digital dial, which hurts its nav use more than you’d think.

To me, it’s a toss-up between the three, but if money is an object and style is not, the fantastic Coros Pace 4 Pro is the winner.

When the first Apple Watch Ultra was released back in 2022, the big tagline (for triathletes, anyway) was: The First Apple Watch That Can Do An Ironman. It was notable because Apple’s previous smartwatches were so heavy on lifestyle features and light on battery power that you literally couldn’t complete a 10-15-hour Ironman wearing one — even if you felt the sports features were robust enough to be helpful, which they weren’t at the time.

In the years since, Apple has consistently produced one of the prettiest, brightest, fastest, and most feature-packed smartwatches for 80% of the population, but even the Ultra line struggled to stand out — especially as the Ultra line made minor changes from version to version: The Ultra 2 brightened the screen, which was nice; the 3 added satellite emergency SOS and a sweeter screen, but almost nothing else. To the latter upgrades, I still maintain that relying on any smartwatch for SOS/satellite comms in the backcountry over a dedicated device like an inReach or even your phone is a very narrow use case and feels extremely reckless, but that’s just me.

But now enter the Ultra 4, which in my opinion is the most relevant upgrade for triathletes since the first version leapt above the Watch Series line. The Ultra 4 has all of the above upgrades but adds some of the most sensitive and accurate heart-rate sensing/physio tracking that I’ve ever used (this is good news for triathletes).

After testing a load of smartwatches this year with sleep tracking that ranges from “good enough” to “seriously I’ve been awake for hours,” only the Ultra 4’s “Overnight Vitals” syncs up with my true sleep cycles and accurately flagged a bad infection that was developing in my leg. I wasn’t even experiencing fever or any outward effects, but the thoughtful (and easy-to-use) combination of very accurate heart rate, accurate sleep cycles, respiratory rate, wrist temperature, and HRV detected the rise and fall of the infection.

I was similarly impressed with the readiness app that helped guide my activity based on vitals and previous activities. Sure, almost every other endurance-focused smartwatch has these features, but none are as accurate and easy to digest.

The last note may seem minor, but it’s not: With the slight increase in battery life, you can now make it through two sleeps before recharging, which means you’re less likely to have to charge overnight or miss/delay a workout while it charges. Yes, 2-3 days is still like 1/8th of most endurance-focused smartwatches, but giving yourself two nights (and a speedier charger that gives you 18 hours in only 15 minutes), it’s finally usable for daily multisport wear and training.

So when you look at the $800-$1,000 price range, you’re looking at smartwatches that do everything and last forever. Up against the $1,000 Garmin Fenix 9, for instance, you’ve got satellite/SOS comms (like the Ultra 4), an AMOLED touchscreen, and pretty much everything else a smartwatch can do — including things like offline voice commands, hands-free calling, an LED flashlight, and more. Most crucially, you’re also getting two weeks or more of battery life to the Ultra 4’s 2-3 days.

That said, if you’re an iPhone user, there is a host of connectivity and lifestyle features that are truly enhanced by the Ultra 4. You can respond to texts, Slacks, sync up everyday mapping and navigation (like when you’re driving around), and way more. No Garmin device (or any other brand) does that with Apple smartphones.

However, if you’re an Android user, the Apple Watch Ultra 4 is wildly overpriced and underpowered because it won’t connect at all with your device (Garmin et al. will). Looking down into the super-competitive $600-ish price range, I’d recommend buyers strongly compare the Ultra 4 to the $600 Suunto Vertical 2 thanks to its LED flashlight and exceptional mapping and battery life. I’d also consider the way overfeatured (almost to a fault) and battery-heavy $650 Amazfit T-Rex Dual Solar.

Ever since I noticed 2025 UTMB race winner Ruth Croft’s Amazfit T-Rex 3 Pro on her wrist a year ago in Chamonix, France, my interest in China-based Amazfit was rekindled. I did a handful of tests on their early endurance-focused efforts, and I felt them to be so beta that I passed on reviewing their models for a few years. Since the T-Rex 3 Pro, however, I’ve kept my eyes peeled for another model that might be interesting for triathletes.

The T-Rex Dual Solar certainly met those standards, with a built-in LED flashlight (think: early morning transition areas or dawn/dusk patrol runs), a surprisingly fast AMOLED (and very bright) screen, enough battery life to get past my magic two-week benchmark, and an almost-ludicrous amount of features, on the same level as a Garmin Fenix, but for at least 30% less money.

First, let’s talk about the most obvious feature on this watch: the dual-sided solar panels. Yes, it seems goofy to have solar panels on the back of the watch, but there are absolutely situations where you might want to try to top up (or at least drain slower) your battery life. I would say in backpacking, this use case comes up pretty often. In triathlon training/life, probably less so: If you’re taking off your watch, you might as well charge the thing, which is infinitely faster than even the best wrist-top solar panels. That said, it is a neat little gimmick.

More importantly, the T-Rex Dual Solar is $150 more than the surprisingly capable T-Rex 3 Pro, but the former doesn’t have a ton more than the latter. Both have two-week-ish battery life, a speaker and microphone, an LED flashlight, rugged styling/durability, and a nearly nauseating host of features — of which a handful are materially useful.

We’re in a time when very few watches do much more than others — with the exception of LED flashlights (which I think are super helpful for triathletes), voice inputting (a mic), and onboard satellite/SOS comms (which I think aren’t that helpful). The T-Rex Dual Solar does everything in that list, except the last, which I don’t find much of a use case for. So then you have to ask, does it do all of those things well? And, are those things easy to use? In the case of the T-Rex Dual Solar, the answer is kind of. User interface and bus were always a little bit of a problem with the first run of Amazfit watches, and while this round is way better, they’re still not as intuitive as a Garmin, Coros, or Apple — the three major competitors.

All that said, if you love a bottomless hole of features, strong battery, LED flashlight, and voice features/functions but don’t want to spend more than $700 and don’t care about a hefty weight and giant wrist footprint, this is it — unless of course you’re good with the T-Rex 3 Pro.

In the $600-plus price range, which I consider the premium range of smartwatches, there’s some pretty tough competition for the Amazfit T-Rex Dual Solar. First, you have the $800 Apple Watch Ultra 4, which gets blown out of the water by the battery life on the T-Rex Solar (and has no LED flashlight), but crushes the Amazfit when it comes to usability and lifestyle features (though irrelevant if you don’t own an iPhone). The latest Ultra also crushes the T-Rex Dual Solar in terms of 24/7 health metrics and physio measuring/monitoring accuracy; the Ultra 4 also has that standalone satellite/SOS comms, and the Amazfit definitely does not.

Above that, the Garmin Fenix 9 comes in around $1,000 and has pretty much everything that the Ultra 4 does, plus an LED flashlight and enough battery life to put up a fight against the T-Rex Dual Solar (though the Garmin would still lose). The Garmin, however, is far more intuitive and easy to use than the Amazfit, and its host of excellent apps (like Spotify, for instance) make it a clear winner. For a Garmin closer in price, the $750 Forerunner 970 also mirrors the T-Rex Dual Solar’s capabilities with easier interfaces (but less battery).

Looking below that, the $400-600 range is also pretty dangerous — especially Amazfit’s own fully capable $400 Amazfit T-Rex 3 Pro that’s virtually identical to the T-Rex Dual Solar if you’re not making lots of use of the backside solar panel. Other than that, there are super capable LED flashlight-equipped watches like the Suunto Vertical 2 ($600) that offer much easier-to-use functions with better companion apps.

There was a time when the Garmin Fenix was pricey, but not out of reach. Less than five years ago you could find a brand-new Fenix 7 for $700. The battery would last close to forever, and there was a chance you’d never use half of the features packed into it. For another $100 or so you could get that all-valuable LED flashlight that used to be unique to the line, but now exists on less-expensive Garmin Instincts, the Suunto Vertical 2, and a few models from Amazfit. You’d get a lot for under $1,000, but you’d still probably not use close to all of it.

Fast forward to today, and the least-expensive Fenix 9 is $1,000. Garmin has added an AMOLED screen to some (and significantly lessened battery life on those models), a speaker/mic, faster map processing, and inReach comm options. If you’re really trying to do an apples-to-apples comparison, the 2022 Fenix 7X Pro Solar ($900 when released) and the 2026 Fenix 9 Pro Solar ($1,300) both have MIP screens and big battery life, but the latter has a mic/speaker (and all that comes with it, like voice control), inReach capabilities built in, and more storage/faster processing. With that in mind (and with the added $8/mo+ cost of the inReach plan), triathletes need to be very thoughtful about how they’re actually going to use the Fenix 9.

Since the inReach capabilities are the newest, shiniest thing across the full Fenix 9 line (and the subscription cost isn’t nothing), triathletes need to think about how often they’d go into an off-grid situation without a smartphone — or actual inReach. If you’re venturing into the rugged backcountry for days on end, you should really arm yourself with a dedicated inReach device, like the $300 Messenger. If you’re not going out for multiple days, most Apple phones now have similar sat features. Barring that, do you really need a no-phone, no-inReach device smartwatch? Probably not.

InReach notwithstanding, the Fenix 9 series feels less novel than it used to be for much more than it used to cost; in the context of the mish-mash featured Fenix 8 line — that had inReach functionality on some models, super-bright MicroLED on others — it feels a little redundant. Of course it has a styling, durability, and construction that Fenix fans will naturally gravitate toward, but at over $1,000 it’s becoming a smaller club than it was.

If we’re looking solely at the MIP-screened (meaning not AMOLED, to be clear) solar version Fenix 9 Pro Solar that costs $1,300, you’re in rare air. None of the Fenix 8s (which are nearly identical to the rest of the Fenix 9 series in many ways) have an MIP screen, so you have to go up against some of the (discounted to under $800) Fenix 7Xs that don’t have inReach. In other brands, you’d be talking about the super long-in-the-tooth $600 Coros Vertix 2 with MIP and a bananas amount of battery, but no LED flashlight or inReach, but an arguably better digital dial for offline mapping use.

The only other watch that’s worth mentioning here is the $800 Apple Watch Ultra 4 that interestingly has onboard SOS/satellite capabilities but also a highly advanced AMOLED touchscreen and nearly incomparable battery life. Even if you look at the AMOLED versions of the Fenix 9 Series that start at $1,000, the Garmins are still blowing the doors off the battery life of the Ultra 4; the Apple claps back with vastly superior lifestyle features (for iPhone users) and a mic/speaker.

All that said, if you can live without inReach (like 99.9% of triathletes can) and a mic/speaker isn’t meaningful to you, now you’re looking at watches for easily half the price, making the whole value proposition pretty tough to stomach. Even the Amazfit T-Rex Dual Solar mentioned here adds a (not-as-good) mic/speaker and has an LED flashlight for $650.

*Tri Battery Life includes the following settings/uses: Always-on display with the lowest possible brightness for bright daylight use; sleep and all-day heart-rate tracking; HRV tracking; 1-2 workouts/day with max GPS accuracy.

The gift tax is one of the most misunderstood parts of the tax code. People hear "gift tax" and assume they'll owe the IRS money for giving a birthday check to their grandchild. That's almost never how it works. The federal gift tax exists to prevent people from giving away their entire estate during their lifetime to dodge estate taxes at death. For the vast majority of Americans, it will never cost them a dime.

Here's what actually matters: in 2026, you can give up to $18,000 to any individual without reporting it to the IRS at all. Give that amount to 10 different people and you've transferred $180,000 completely under the radar. Go above the annual limit and you still won't owe tax — you'll just file a form that tracks the excess against your $13.61 million lifetime exemption.

The gift tax is really a planning tool, not a penalty. Understanding how it works can help you transfer wealth to family members, fund education, reduce your taxable estate, and accelerate your heirs' path to financial independence — all without triggering any actual tax.

The annual gift tax exclusion is the amount you can give to any single recipient each year without needing to file a gift tax return or use any of your lifetime exemption. For 2026, that amount is $18,000 per recipient.

This limit applies per giver, per recipient. That means:

The IRS adjusts this amount for inflation periodically. Here's how the annual exclusion has changed over the years:

The annual exclusion has roughly doubled since 2002, when it was just $11,000. Inflation adjustments are made in $1,000 increments, so the number stays flat for a year or two, then bumps up.

This is the single most important gift tax fact: the person making the gift is responsible for any gift tax — never the recipient. If your grandmother gives you $50,000, she files the gift tax return and uses her lifetime exemption. You don't report it as income, you don't owe tax on it, and you don't need to do anything. Gifts received are not taxable income.

When you give more than the annual exclusion to any single person, the excess counts against your lifetime gift and estate tax exemption — currently $13.61 million per person ($27.22 million for married couples). You won't actually owe gift tax until you've exceeded this lifetime amount.

Let's put that in perspective. If you give your daughter $118,000 in one year, you're $100,000 over the annual exclusion. You file Form 709 to report it, and the IRS subtracts that $100,000 from your lifetime exemption. Your remaining exemption drops from $13.61 million to $13.51 million. No tax is owed.

At the 40% top gift tax rate, you'd need to give away more than $13.61 million over your lifetime before any actual tax kicks in. That puts fewer than 0.1% of Americans in gift tax territory.

Important sunset warning: The current $13.61 million exemption is set to be cut roughly in half on January 1, 2026, reverting to approximately $7 million per person (adjusted for inflation) under the Tax Cuts and Jobs Act sunset provisions. This has created urgency for high-net-worth families to make large gifts before the window closes.

Several types of transfers are completely excluded from gift tax rules — no annual limit, no lifetime exemption usage, no Form 709 required:

The education and medical exclusions are especially powerful for the FI community. A grandparent can pay $50,000 in tuition directly to a university AND give the grandchild $18,000 in cash in the same year — all tax-free with no reporting.

If you give more than $18,000 to any single recipient in a year, you must file IRS Form 709 (United States Gift and Generation-Skipping Transfer Tax Return) with your tax return. Filing Form 709 does not mean you owe tax — it simply reports the gift and tracks your lifetime exemption usage.

One of the most powerful gift tax strategies available is the 529 plan 5-year election. The IRS allows you to front-load up to 5 years of annual exclusion gifts into a 529 education savings plan in a single year.

For 2026, that means you can contribute up to $90,000 (5 x $18,000) to a 529 plan for a single beneficiary in one year. A married couple electing gift splitting can contribute up to $180,000 per beneficiary.

The catch: if you use the 5-year election and then pass away during the 5-year period, a prorated portion of the gift returns to your taxable estate.

The gift tax and estate tax share the same $13.61 million lifetime exemption. Think of it as one pool of money that covers both gifts during your life and transfers at death.

Every dollar of lifetime exemption you use for gifts during your life reduces the amount available to shelter your estate from tax at death. However, there's a strategic advantage to giving during your lifetime: future appreciation on gifted assets escapes your taxable estate.

Example: You give your daughter stock worth $1 million today. You use $982,000 of lifetime exemption ($1M minus $18K annual exclusion). If that stock grows to $3 million by the time you die, the full $3 million — including $2 million in appreciation — is completely outside your estate. That's $2 million that will never be subject to estate tax.
