#8938. When Yoga Studios Abruptly Close, What Happens to Students and Teachers?

On September 9, Y7 yoga teacher Aanch Khaneja showed up at the Silver Lake studio in Los Angeles to teach class and encountered a locked gate. Y7 Teachers in New York, Los Angeles, and Austin similarly showed up to class and found the studios closed. That afternoon, after longtime Y7 member Andrew Johnston received an email stating the studio was “now closed,” he showed up at the Silver Lake location anyway for the 5:30 p.m. class. He encountered Khaneja “on her phone finding out that it had unceremoniously shuttered.”

Two weeks later, on September 23, a similar situation was unfolding across the Atlantic at London’s Triyoga, a fixture of the city’s yoga scene for the last 25 years. “There was a note on the door simply saying the center was closed,” says student Katie Puckrik, an American broadcaster and writer based in London. She had shown up for class after being unable to book class online or reach anyone at the studio by phone.

As she paused and processed the situation, another student arrived at Triyoga after receiving an email notification that the studio was “closed until further notice.” Puckrik explains that the other student was a new member and had just bought a year’s membership.

And the month before, the YUJ chain of yoga and wellness studios in Paris surprised longtime students and teachers by closing its doors following its liquidation on August 13. Teachers were reportedly informed via WhatsApp and the studio’s home page was updated to read, “Merci et au revoir.” Beneath that message, there is a letter from founder Hélène Duval expressing appreciation for 12 years and regret for those who had purchased memberships or class packages, which she says were now questions for the court-appointed liquidator.

In each instance, teachers from each studio remain unpaid for their final weeks and, in some instances, months of work. That includes more than 200 Y7 staff, per a Substack written by Y7 founder Sarah Larson Levey, approximately 100 Triyoga teachers, according to an article in The Guardian, and some 50 YUJ teachers, per Le Parisien.

Students who had paid upfront for class packages or unlimited class memberships that remain unused have also received little, if any, clarity as to whether there will be reimbursement.

Many affected by the shutdowns took to Instagram to express their shock, frustration, and concerns. Some Y7 students and teachers left comments on the studio’s recent Instagram posts, with dozens expressing dismay over the abrupt shutdown. Many criticized the company for not responding to refund requests from students and shared suggestions on how to attempt to secure compensation for unused classes. Others expressed frustration about missing paychecks. Some teachers took it upon themselves to leave comments apologizing for the lack of communication by the company.

Everyone was left not knowing what happens now regarding prepaid memberships and unpaid wages.

“A sudden closure isn’t, in and of itself, necessarily an illegal act,” says Jennifer Mohamed, a New Jersey-based yoga teacher and business attorney who drafts membership and employment agreements, among other services. “It just feels icky.”

Mohamed explains that the specific circumstances of each closure determine the legal options for teachers and students seeking back pay or refunds.

Mohamed says that if bankruptcy is declared in the U.S., secured lenders are prioritized, followed by employees’ outstanding wages, and, to a lesser extent, customers’ prepaid deposits. Without bankruptcy, there is no formal court process to sort out who gets paid first, according to Mohamed.

Lacking bankruptcy, any potential recourse following a studio shutdown depends on the specific circumstances of each situation. In London and Paris, laws regarding the closures of businesses vary from those in the U.S., yet in general, employees receive more protection than independent contractors when a business shuts down. Yet it can be unclear regarding how compensation works for students who prepaid for classes.

Vincent Miceli of VM Fitness, which had taken over operations of the Y7 heated vinyasa brand seven weeks earlier, did not respond to a request for a comment. The website and email for the fitness group Common Bond, which operated Triyoga, appear to no longer be functioning.

Abrupt closures are the worst-case scenario. But a yoga studio can make a graceful exit. When Kelly Elle Kenworthy decided to shut the doors of the independently operated Little Yoga Studio in Boulder, Colorado, in 2025, she informed everyone in an email a little less than two weeks in advance, encouraging students to avail themselves of the studio until its last class. In her farewell, she conveyed there would be no refunds but that unused credits would be “received as a donation toward the studio’s closing costs,” which included teachers’ final paychecks.

When unexpected shutdowns happen, there are ways to minimize potential loss for those who take and teach classes, explains Mohamed, who is not representing any parties connected with the recent studio closures. The following information is based primarily on  U.S-specific law and is not intended as legal advice. Regulations vary by state and country as well as specific situations.

1. Pay for your membership by credit card rather than debit

If a yoga studio closes and doesn’t respond to a query or issue a refund, you can request that your credit card issuer reverse the charge for services you never received. However, credit card disputes have deadlines, so file as soon as you know the studio isn’t reopening. Debit cards and payment apps offer far less protection.

Johnston, who held a monthly membership with Y7, disputed his final charge with his credit card company, a tactic many commenters on Y7’s Instagram page suggested. He received a reinstatement of his funds.

Derek Chisamore had prepaid for an annual Y7 membership with two months remaining at the time of the company’s closure. Despite receiving an email from Miceli assuring him that students would be refunded, Chisamore has yet to receive anything. He eventually reached out to his credit card company and received “a prorated charge back for the time missed.”

2. Save a copy of your membership agreement

Prepaying for yoga classes that go unused because a studio closes may fall under a breach-of-contract claim. “If you’ve purchased services that then cannot be fulfilled, the law is gonna say, ‘Well, there’s a breach of contract here because you didn’t get what you bargained for,’” says Mohamed. In that instance, it might be possible to seek compensation for what is owed.

In order to prove breach of contract, you need the agreement. When you electronically sign your membership, the studio typically sends a copy of it to your email. Mohamed recommends keeping it somewhere safe, whether you download it right away or file it in a saved email folder. If you signed your agreement months ago and can not find it, check the studio’s app for a copy or request it from the front desk. A closed studio can’t send you a copy of your contract.

Check if the agreement terms regarding refunds might be listed in your policy. Also, look to see if the studio lists a specific timeframe for answering refund requests and if there is an arbitration clause, which can bar you from suing in court or joining other members in a class action.

Some states in the U.S. have health club laws that protect members’ prepaid fees, but yoga studios often fall outside them, explains Mohamed.

For example, New York’s Health Club Services Act is written broadly and covers businesses offering instruction in “physical fitness” or “well-being,” so it could arguably apply to yoga studios, Mohamed says. In practice, though, no yoga studios are registered with the New York Department of State, which suggests the state hasn’t required them to comply.

With more studios moving to memberships, Mohamed says, “This may be an area where we see change in the future.” You can research whether your state has a health club law and whether it covers single-discipline studios.

For teachers who did not receive paychecks for work following a studio shutdown, much depends on the status as either employee or independent contractor, according to Mohamed.

1. Know and understand your employment status

Receiving a W-2 tends as an employee to offer teachers more protections than a form 1099 as an independent contractor.

Yoga teachers who are classified as independent contractors are not guaranteed coverage of lost wages in the U.S., although they may be able to sue for breach of contract. Although the laws vary by country, more than 100 Triyoga teachers have sought support in recovering wages via the Independent Workers’ Union of Great Britain (IWGB) Yoga Teachers Union, according to the International Business Times.

Employees may be able to file a wage claim with their state labor department, apply for unemployment, and join class-action lawsuits when a studio shuts down and fails to compensate them for work delivered, says Mohamed.

Some teachers from Y7 in Los Angeles have been filing individual wage claims with the California Labor Commissioner’s Office, according to Khaneja. Successful unpaid-wage claims could bring penalties that double or even triple what’s owed, depending on the state in which they are filed. In an August 20 email to staff, Miceli acknowledged that “applicable penalties” under state wage laws would apply to late pay.

2. Review the fine print of your contract

Check your contract to confirm when you get paid and what notice or payment you’re owed if classes are canceled or the studio closes. Ideally, read this carefully before you sign.

Look for non-compete clauses, too. Depending on your state, they can limit where you teach next. California and a handful of other states ban them outright, while others enforce them only if they’re reasonable in time and distance.

3. Keep up-to-date records of hours and expenses

Don’t rely on the studio’s scheduling app or payroll system for verification of your teaching hours. Keep your own record of every class you teach. If the company suddenly shuts down, you might lose access to these systems and the listing of classes for which you were—and were not—paid.

Also, independently track any expenses the studio owes you, such as costs related to a workshop or training that you led.

There were signals that something was off at the studios in the weeks leading up to the abrupt closures, according to several teachers.

Starting in July, payroll at Y7 was delayed multiple times. “They kept emailing saying, ‘You will get paid on Friday.’ And then on Friday they were like, ‘You will get paid on Monday.’ And then on Monday they were like, ‘You will get paid next Friday,’” says Khaneja. “They just kept pushing it off again and again.” The evening Y7 studios closed, teachers received an email from Miceli notifying them of the closure.

Similarly, Triyoga teachers say their pay was delayed again and again. “They would never guarantee the payment was coming, and they were never willing to say anything,” says Adam Husler, a longtime Triyoga senior teacher. He decided to quit two weeks prior to the studio’s shutdown because the company couldn’t guarantee funding for a yoga teacher training that he was about to co-lead.

Late pay doesn’t always mean a studio is about to close, but it does caution you to pay attention. Many teachers diversify their income streams with other types of work so they have fallback plans in case of studio closures.

There’s another kind of loss that accompanies the abrupt closure of a yoga studio beyond financial. There’s the loss of one’s practice and favored teachers. The loss of community and connection from no longer moving and breathing with the same crowd week after week. And there’s an emotional loss.

“Triyoga was where I went to release and recharge,” says Puckrik. “The staff became friends, and the lobby became a home away from home.”

In Los Angeles, Chisamore is also grieving. “I know it is crazy to say, but it feels like someone died,” he says. “I lost the routine that I had for years without a sense of closure. I did not even get to say goodbye. Not only do I miss them, but I feel badly that they still have not been paid for their hard work and talents.” He has since connected with a few teachers on social media and hopes to practice with them again soon.

Yet as students and teachers start to recreate their practice elsewhere, the larger yoga community has stepped in to support those left stranded without a home studio.

In London, Home Wellness, founded by Triyoga’s original founder, Jonathan Sattin, and Mission, started by a former Triyoga yoga director, Genny Wilkinson, are honoring the remaining memberships of students, according to Puckrik. Down To Earth Yoga turned its Instagram into a kind of “bulletin board” for displaced Triyoga teachers and the students searching for them. It’s also offering several free classes to students with the message, “No membership, no commitment—just somewhere to land while you work out what comes next.”

In Paris, the former YUJ location at the Hôtel HoY reopened under different management. It invites those with unfulfilled YUJ memberships to reach out and inquire about transferring their missing classes, with decisions made on a case-by-case basis.

Former Y7 student Johnston now practices at Indigo Fitness in Los Angeles, where he is not only rebuilding his yoga practice but, hopefully, his community. An instructor at the studio recently asked him for recommendations as to which Y7 teachers the studio should hire. “So hopefully I’ll see some of them again very soon,” he says.

Support for Y7 teachers has also come from an unexpected place. Anne Mahlum, founder of the boutique fitness chain Solidcore, has reportedly offered to pay outstanding wages totalling close to $123,000 through individual GoFundMe pages set up by individual teachers.

Some teachers left without a home studio are instead going grassroots. Literally. Khaneja and several other former Y7 teachers quickly formed the Sunset Movement Collective and currently teach yoga and sculpt outdoors in a park every week.

“A lot of the students are still showing up,” she says. “We’re just trying to take something from what was taken from us.”

A primary beneficiary is the person or entity you designate to receive an asset — such as a life insurance policy, 401(k), IRA, or bank account — when you die. If you name multiple primary beneficiaries, they split the asset according to the percentages you specify. A contingent beneficiary (also called a secondary or backup beneficiary) receives the asset only if all primary beneficiaries are unable to inherit, either because they predeceased you, disclaimed the inheritance, or cannot be located.

This layered system exists because life is unpredictable. If you name your spouse as primary beneficiary on your life insurance and you both die in the same accident, the contingent beneficiary ensures the proceeds go where you intended rather than into your general estate where they become subject to probate.

You can name individuals, trusts, charities, or even your estate as a beneficiary. However, naming your estate is generally a poor choice because it forces the asset through probate, exposing it to creditors, delays, and court costs. The entire purpose of a beneficiary designation is to transfer assets outside of probate — naming your estate defeats that advantage.

When naming multiple beneficiaries, you must choose a distribution method that determines what happens if one beneficiary dies before you. This choice is critical and frequently misunderstood.

Per stirpes (Latin for "by the branch") means each branch of your family tree receives its designated share. If your son predeceases you, his share passes down to his children (your grandchildren) in equal portions. The family branch stays intact.

Per capita (Latin for "by the head") means assets are divided equally among surviving beneficiaries only. If your son predeceases you, his share is redistributed among your other surviving beneficiaries — his children receive nothing.

For most families, per stirpes is the safer default because it prevents accidental disinheritance of grandchildren. If you want surviving beneficiaries to absorb the shares of those who predecease you, per capita achieves that — but make sure that outcome aligns with your actual wishes.

Some financial institutions also offer per capita at each generation, which distributes equally among the nearest living generation first, then passes remaining shares equally to the next generation. This hybrid approach is less common but available at some custodians.

Beneficiary designations are deceptively simple forms that create binding legal consequences. The most expensive mistakes happen not from malice but from neglect.

In most states, a divorce does not automatically remove your ex-spouse from beneficiary designations on retirement accounts or life insurance policies. Federal law (ERISA) governs employer-sponsored plans like 401(k)s, and ERISA does not recognize state divorce revocation statutes. If you divorce and never update your 401(k) beneficiary, your ex-spouse can legally claim the entire balance — even if your will leaves everything to your new spouse.

Minor children cannot legally receive life insurance proceeds or retirement account distributions. If you name a 5-year-old as beneficiary, the insurance company will not release funds until a court appoints a guardian or conservator of the child's property. This process costs $2,000 to $5,000 in legal fees, takes months, and requires ongoing court reporting. Instead, name a trust for the benefit of the child or use your state's Uniform Transfers to Minors Act (UTMA) custodial designation.

If you leave the beneficiary field blank or all named beneficiaries predecease you without a contingent, the asset typically defaults to your estate. This triggers probate, adds 6 to 18 months of delay, and exposes the asset to estate creditors. Always name at least one contingent beneficiary.

Your beneficiary designations and your will can contradict each other. The beneficiary designation always wins. If your will says your daughter gets your IRA but the IRA beneficiary form still names your brother, your brother gets the IRA. Review both documents together annually.

Free calculators, a personalized FI roadmap, and a community of 25K+ on the same journey.

Set a recurring calendar reminder to review every beneficiary designation once per year — ideally alongside your tax preparation. Pull statements from your 401(k), IRA, life insurance, bank accounts, and brokerage accounts. Verify that primary and contingent designations match your current wishes. This 30-minute annual review prevents the kind of outdated-beneficiary disasters that lead to costly litigation and assets going to unintended recipients.

Yes. You can name multiple primary beneficiaries and assign a percentage to each. For example, you could name three children as primary beneficiaries at 33.3% each. The percentages must total 100%.

If all primary beneficiaries predecease you and no contingent is named, the asset typically defaults to your estate. This forces the asset through probate, where it is subject to creditor claims, court costs, and delays of 6 to 18 months.

For state-law-governed accounts like IRAs and life insurance, some states have revocation-upon-divorce statutes — but not all. For ERISA-governed accounts like employer 401(k)s, federal law does not recognize state divorce revocation. You must manually update the beneficiary form after divorce to be safe.

Yes. A beneficiary can file a qualified disclaimer within 9 months of the account holder's death. The disclaimed asset then passes to the contingent beneficiary or according to the plan's default rules. Disclaimers are sometimes used for tax planning purposes.

Naming a trust provides control over how and when assets are distributed — especially useful for minor children, spendthrift beneficiaries, or blended families. However, trusts named as IRA beneficiaries must meet specific IRS requirements to qualify for stretch distributions under the SECURE Act. Consult an estate planning attorney before naming a trust as retirement account beneficiary.

A POD designation on a bank account functions exactly like a beneficiary designation. The named person receives the account balance upon your death without going through probate. You maintain full control of the account during your lifetime and can change the POD beneficiary at any time.

Primary and contingent beneficiary designations are among the most powerful — and most overlooked — estate planning tools. They transfer assets instantly upon death, bypass probate entirely, and override your will in every state. The 30 minutes it takes to review and update your designations after every major life event can save your family months of legal proceedings, thousands in attorney fees, and the heartbreak of assets going to unintended recipients.

#8932. The Very Best Yoga Mats Under $50

(Photo: Thomas Barwick | Getty; All in Motion; Canva)

Looking for the best inexpensive yoga mats? With the following picks from our expert testers, you’ll experience more than sufficient grip and cushiness while keeping to a budget. The standouts are the Gaiam Premium 5mm Yoga Mat ($24), which is the best yoga mat for beginners, and the All in Motion Peak Rubber Yoga Mat ($35) for the best overall inexpensive yoga mat, especially for hot yoga. Whether you’re new to yoga or simply don’t want to spend a lot of money, these are the most reliable options to consider.

No one talks about this. But you can experience some serious B-rated horror movie moments when you practice on a lot of yoga mats. Your hands slowly and inexorably sliding forward as you try to find stillness in Down Dog. Your mat wrinkling and sliding beneath you as you attempt to transition from Low Lunge into Warrior 2. It’s enough to make you want to silently and helplessly scream.

You would think that throwing money at the problem helps. And I’m not gonna lie, sometimes it can when you splurge on stand-out yoga mats that support you in ways that are unspeakably better than other mats. But not every absurdly expensive mat ensures you avoid these cringe situations. Just as not every inexpensive mat guarantees you’ll experience challenges. And not everyone wants to or is able to spend a lot of money on a mat. And until you’ve actually practiced on a mat, it’s pretty much impossible to discern what it’s like.

So we did the testing for you. I spent the first decade of my yoga practice on a $17 mat quite similar to one of the selections below, and throughout the next decade of my yoga practice, I’ve slipped, slided, and sweated my way through poses on dozens of different yoga mats in all price ranges, and so have our other testers of all experience levels. In so doing, we’ve culled the options for spending less than $50 down to the two most reliable, decidedly non-nightmarish, unequivocally best inexpensive yoga mats.

Because you don’t need to let price deter you from your practice, whether you’re a beginner or simply someone who thinks of everything else you could put that extra money toward (ie your electric bill, groceries, those vintage 90s cargo pants on Poshmark that you can’t stop thinking about). You just need to avoid the ones that make you question your decision to try yoga. Instead, you should simply be questioning your discretion in choosing a mat.

Here’s everything you need to know to make the right decision.

Material: Latex-free PVC Thickness: 5mm Dimensions: 68 x 24 inches Weight: 2.6 pounds

Pros and Cons + Sufficiently sturdy, grippy + cushy + Ethereally lightweight + Price! – Slightly slippery, especially when wet – Smaller dimensions than most mats

This is what you buy when you want to spend as little as possible on a mat that delivers rather than disappoints. Not surprisingly, it’s from longtime mat maker Gaiam, which offers dozens of styles, although the Premium 5mm is my choice for its textured surface, decent enough traction for hands and feet even during arm balancing, and spongy cushiness that lets you sink ever so slightly into the mat.

Although it’s not as densely cushioned as most more expensive mats, the Premium 5mm was preferred by beginners who found the texture to be reassuringly supportive during standing postures and sufficiently comfortable during shapes that require kneeling, sitting, or reclining. That said, if you think you’ll practice primarily yin or restorative yoga, in which you’re sitting or lying on your mat the entire class, you might want something cushier.

Look, it’s not flawless. In testing during recent years, it sometimes wrinkled slightly beneath my feet as I transitioned, although not in an overly distracting way. It sometimes felt as though my hands or feet were beginning to slide on the slick surface, but not to the extreme experienced on other mats in this price category. Although when practiced on during heated or sweaty conditions, that slide factor increased, so consider yourself warned. As for longevity, if you end up practicing several times a week, the mat might show signs of the surface wearing down wherever you commonly place hands and feet, although Gaiam does offer a lifetime guarantee.

Whatever the mat lacks in longevity, it more than makes up for in lightweightness. At just 2.6 pounds, it’s easy to lug along with you to class, even if you walk several city blocks to a studio or gym. (Trust me, pricier mats get heavy quite quickly.) Part of that seeming weightlessness might be due to the fact that it’s a couple inches narrower than a lot of mats, making for a slightly constricted experience in terms of square footage beneath you during your practice.

The mat is made of PVC. Some retailers refer to the material as “non-toxic,” which might sound like an anomaly. Gaiam’s website states it is made without the phthalates DEHP, DBP, BBP, DINP, DIDP and DNOP.

This is almost the same Gaiam mat that I started practicing on years ago, and although I haven’t used the ones I’ve tried in recent years for as long, at some point they, too, seem to start showing signs of wear in places where I regularly place my hands and feet. I don’t regret having chosen Gaiam and I strongly encourage others do the same. But if I had to do it again, I’d know when to let it go.

Bottom Line: It’s an inexpensive yoga mat that’s ideal for anyone curious to try yoga but not certain if they’ll want to stick with it in the long run. Or someone who practices occasionally, whether at home or at a studio or gym. Or as a suitable stand-in for someone who’s still deciding what, exactly, they prefer in a pricier mat before making that commitment.

Material: Polyurethane + rubber Thickness: 5mm Dimensions: 68 x 26 inches Weight: TK

Pros and Cons + Grippy surface + Doesn’t wrinkle or slide on the floor + Comparable to mats twice its cost – Heavy – Surface scratches easily

The Peak has a sleek surface, quite similar to that of more expensive brands designed for hot yoga that cost exponentially more. (IYKYK.) If I didn’t know better, I’d guess it cost closer to $100 based on how well it handles during my intermittent usage of it during vinyasa practices the last couple years.

The mat literally did not budge beneath me during any sort of transition in between poses thanks to its rubber base that practically adhered the hardwood floor beneath it. And don’t be fooled by that smooth polyurethane surface, because it capably held my hands and feet in place, even when sweating or in a heated space.

The mat also brings a dense cushiness, one that doesn’t feel spongy, unstable, imbalanced, or anything other than supportive and amply comfortable for seated and reclined poses. I’ve practiced yin yoga on it and had no complaints.

It is heavy, though. So you probably want to commute with it in the trunk rather than carrying it along sidewalks. And that sleek surface doesn’t remain unscathed if, like me, you have four-pawed friends who like to stretch their claws beneath you while you’re in Down Dog or Warrior 2. But the rest of the mat is as rugged as its heft would suggest. Mine has no signs of breaking down so far.

Bottom Line: When you want durability or just a decent grip to see you through any style of practice, this is the most acceptable mat priced below $50.

Not surprisingly, there are caveats for any inexpensive yoga mat that costs less than $50. So depending on how you practice, perhaps you think of the mat as one that’s “enough.” As in, cushy enough. Grippy enough. Supportive enough. And good enough to keep you from being distracted by what’s happening beneath you as you practice. Because as much as I appreciate the way these mats handle for the money, they are not designed the same as mats that cost exponentially more. Adjust your expectations accordingly.

Also, and importantly, neither of these mats is an altogether sustainable option. (With my sincerest apologies to the planet.) If eco-friendly options are a priority for you, rest assured, you can find an array of yoga mats, although most are in the $60-plus realm.

Consider, though, that sustainability can be defined in several ways. If either of the above mats meets your short-term needs yet ultimately ends up being your starter mat rather than your long-term mat, you can always donate it to a local school, community center, studio, or thrift store and let it become someone else’s starter mat. That, too, is sustainability. Or if that mat has become worn in ways you wouldn’t want to practice on, neither will someone else. In that case, repurpose it around the house or donate it to a local animal shelter.

Three years ago, we looked beyond the mats we typically practice on and canvassed online comments from users for dozens and dozens of brands of yoga mats of all price points. Then we asked 18 yoga students and teachers of all experience levels with yoga to try various yoga mats that received the highest ratings. And each year since then, we look to see which mats are surging in popularity or new to the market and test those as well. This year, we took special interest in budget options that might not have made our list of overall best, and took into consideration our experience while standing, transitioning, balancing, kneeling, sitting, and reclining on several mats.

#8931. Transform Your Core with This 10-Minute Exercise Ball Workout

An exercise (or stability) ball is an inexpensive but effective strength training tool for triathletes. (Photo: Getty Images)

For this article, retired pro triathlete and Triathlete contributor Emma-Kate Lidbury spoke to strength coach and former pro Dede Griesbauer about why this stability ball workout is so effective for triathletes.

Here’s the thing about strength training for triathletes: Almost nobody skips it because they don’t believe in it. They skip it because of the drive to the gym or the 90 minutes that don’t exist between that threshold bike workout and school pickup.

So what if we make life a little easier and remove some of the barriers to getting strength done?

This routine does exactly that and requires one piece of equipment – an exercise ball – and a patch of floor about the size of a yoga mat. No need for dumbbells, a bench, a gym membership, or the drive there. You can pick up an exercise ball for about the same price as a mid-range pair of goggles; it can fit into most any suitcase; and it might just help you find every stabilizer muscle you’ve quietly neglected since your last off-season strength block.

A stability ball is, by design, unstable. That’s the entire value proposition. It offers the following benefits:

Every exercise here demands you hold a neutral spine against something actively trying to move you out of it. Former pro triathlete turned strength coach Dede Griesbauer points out that this pays off in two places triathletes care about: run efficiency, and the ability to hold a stable position in the aerobars.

With an exercise like the rear foot elevated lunge (below), Griesbauer notes this forces each leg to work independently, which may reveal the left-right discrepancies a bilateral squat lets you hide. This matters for power balance on the bike and for not favoring one side on the run, which can help reduce injury risk.

Almost every movement in this routine trains multiple muscle groups at once. Griesbauer’s summary: It offers good “bang for the buck” with minimal equipment, minimal space, and minimal setup.

Griesbauer advises adding strength work to your hard days, not because it’s pleasant to stack lifting onto a threshold run, but because the alternative – sprinkling it across easy days – erodes the recovery that those days are designed to deliver.

“Make your hard days hard so that your easy days can be easy,” she says.

That’s the ideal. Griesbauer is also clear about what “ideal” might look like for an age-grouper with a job.

“Not everyone will have time to do their hard bike or run session AND make time for strength on the same day,” she says. “The good news is that this session isn’t heavy loading. These are good basic movements, so if you are time-crunched, adding them wherever you can is better than not doing them at all.”

Two sessions a week is the target, but once isn’t a failure. “Some is better than none,” Griesbauer says, “so if you can only do it once? Get it done once.”

Start with a single pass through all nine exercises (which should take approximately 10-12 minutes).

Once one round stops feeling like work, add a second. Then, if time allows, add a third. Three circuits should take you about 30-35 minutes and is plenty of stimulus for a routine that isn’t loading you heavily. Rest 30 to 60 seconds between exercises and a couple of minutes between rounds.

Progress through the workout in the order listed. It moves between lower body, core, and upper body so nothing fatigues to failure.

Stand on your right foot with your left leg extended behind you and the top of your left foot resting on the ball. Bend your right knee until your right thigh is parallel to the floor, keeping your torso upright and your weight on your heel. Now press your heel into the floor and return to the start position. Complete 10 repetitions and then repeat the exercise with your left leg.

Begin in a prone position with the tops of your feet resting on the ball, your palms on the floor underneath your shoulders, and your body forming a straight line. Now contract your stomach muscles, bend your knees, and roll the ball toward your chest. Pause briefly and roll the ball back until your body forms a straight line again. Complete 12 repetitions.

Assume a modified push-up position with your feet together, your body forming a perfectly straight line and your palms positioned slightly more than shoulder-width apart on the ball. Bend your elbows and smoothly lower your chest to within an inch of the ball. Immediately press back upward to the start position. If you have difficulty doing a full push-up, do a half push-up, bending your elbows only to 90 degrees before pressing upward. Complete 10 repetitions.

Start in a bridge position, face up, with your head and shoulders on the floor and your heels resting on top of the ball, your body suspended in a straight line between these points. Contract your hamstrings and roll the ball toward your butt. Pause briefly and extend your legs, rolling the ball back to the starting point. Don’t let your hips drop. Complete 12 repetitions. If this exercise is too easy, do a single-leg version, elevating one foot above the ball and pulling the ball toward your butt with the other leg.

Kneel on the floor facing the ball, lean forward slightly, and place your forearms on top of the ball. Pull your belly button toward your spine. Slowly roll the ball forward by extending your forearms out in front of you and allowing your body to tilt toward the floor. Concentrate on maintaining perfect alignment of your spine. Stop just before you’re forced to arch your back. Hold this position for a two-count and then return to the start position, exhaling as you do so. Complete 12 repetitions.

Lie facedown on the ball with your palms on the floor. Begin with the ball supporting your pelvic area. Now use your hands to drag your body forward over the ball until it is underneath the tops of your feet, keeping your body in a straight line. Pause briefly and roll back to the start position. Complete 10 repetitions.

Assume a modified push-up position with your palms on the floor, the tops of your feet resting on the ball, and your body in a perfectly straight line between them. Bend your elbows and lower your chest toward the floor. Go as far as you can without strain; it’s OK if it isn’t very far. Now press back to the start position. Complete 10 repetitions.

Lie face up with your upper back supported by the ball, your feet flat on the floor about 12 inches apart, your knees bent and your body forming a “tabletop” from knees to chest. Contract your calf muscles and raise your heels off the floor without allowing your hips to sag. Now lower your heels back to the floor. Complete 12 repetitions. If this exercise is too easy, do a single-leg version, first crossing your left ankle over your right knee and then doing the reverse.

Get into a plank position with your palms on the floor underneath your chest and the ball supporting your shins. Keeping your arms straight, press the heels of your palms into the floor and push your body backward so that the ball rolls up under your thighs. Go as far as you can and then pull your body in the opposite direction until you’re back in the start position. Complete 12 repetitions. If this exercise is too easy, start with the ball under the tops of your feet.

Instability is the point, which also means this routine isn’t universally appropriate. Griesbauer flags a few pointers worth knowing before you start. Note that none of these are a reason not to train. They just require you to adapt or swap movements if needed.

If you have a cranky lower back: The abdominal rollout generates high spinal extension and shear force if your core gives out mid-rep, which can be a genuine problem for anyone with disc history. The reverse crunch can pull you into loaded lumbar flexion if control slips, and a hamstring curl performed with dropped hips will arch and cramp the low back.

If you have “shoulder history”: Push-ups on a moving ball tax the rotator cuff hard, and the ball walk-out places prolonged, shifting load on the shoulder joint. Skip both if you’ve dealt with instability or impingement.

If you have wrist issues: The ball’s spherical surface forces the wrists into deep extension while the weight moves under you. Elevated push-ups shift more bodyweight forward onto the same joints.

If you have knees and hip flexor problems: The rear foot elevated lunge loads the front knee in deep flexion and stretches the trailing leg aggressively, which can be enough to tip the pelvis if your hip flexors are tight. Tight hip flexors will also hijack the reverse crunch from the lower abs.

If you have cramp-prone calves and hamstrings: The bridge heel raise fires the calves while the hamstrings are already shortened, which is a reliable spasm trigger. The hamstring curl frequently cramps athletes with weak hamstrings on the concentric.

If you have compromised balance: Any single-leg work raises fall risk. Have a wall or chair within reach if you feel you might need it.

#8926. Everything You Need to Know About Safely Practicing Standing Forward Bend

(Photo: Andrew Clark | Design in Canva by Laura Harold)

In Yoga Journal’s Archives series, we share a curated collection of articles originally published in past issues beginning in 1975. This article about how to do Standing Forward Bend first appeared in the May-June 2001 issue of Yoga Journal. You can find more of our Archives here.

In most contemporary societies, we are frequently exposed to confrontation—in our environments, in our relationships, in our jobs. When we lack the tools to deal skillfully with confrontation, our systems begin to contract—mentally, emotionally, and physically. When ignored for too long this contraction can color the way we perceive our “reality.” What is very unnatural to a healthy body can begin to seem natural.

Because this process occurs over extended periods of time, like the aging process, we often lack the awareness that it is happening until we are beyond simple fixes. With recognition and practice, though, this contraction can be used to create the “in-tense(ness)” necessary to overcome distortions in perception, enabling us to view confrontation as a useful, often necessary, component of growth.

Consider Uttanasana (Standing Forward Bend). If you are a beginner, whether you are stiff or flexible, this pose will likely take your attention directly into areas of your body that are unfamiliar, painful, and/or unresponsive. Stiff practitioners have to learn to work with pain, which is often intense, in order to remove obstructions found in the legs and hips in this pose. Less flexible beginners often struggle with the opposing forces of particular actions in a pose when they first encounter it. Attempting to relax muscles is not easy when you are receiving a steady stream (or scream) of more demanding messages in the seemingly undecipherable language of pain. It may feel like the resistance you experience is protecting you from injury or “overdoing.”

The Sanskrit word ut can be defined as intense but also as a point of indicated deliberation. By its very nature (and its name), Uttanasana takes us on a confrontational journey toward overcoming ingrained resistance and penetrating the dense matter of our consciousness. For those with chronically tight hamstrings and/or hips, the pose forces the mind into a very alert state and fills the “gaps” typically found in a beginner’s attention. This is a very important place to be. In it, you are given an opportunity to feel the physical power and observe the dynamics of a stressful situation, and to overcome the mental or emotional struggle inherent in that predicament.

Entering the pose requires a little preparation, and in the event of pre-existing lower back conditions, a couple of modifications may also be beneficial. If you practice in the early morning, it’s a good idea to get the spine warmed up first. (A little hot water focused on your spine for a few minutes in the shower can never hurt, although your utility bills might ache a little.) A simple way to set up the spine for forward bending in Uttanasana is to sit first in a cross-legged position and bend forward. This should give the hips a wake-up call.

From the sitting position, move into Downward-Facing Dog, which begins the process of lengthening the back of the legs and continues the work of elongating the spine. From Down Dog, with an exhalation, step or jump your feet to your hands, and as you inhale, slowly straighten your legs, keeping your hands on the floor. Lift your spine as you gaze forward. Feel the inhalation fill the back of your lungs, and as the back lungs and ribs expand, let the sensation of this lift support the movement in your thoracic spine.

As the spine lifts, feel a downward pressure on the hips and, catching that sensation, press the top of the hip bones (iliac crest) down firmly.

As you exhale, release your head and the weight of your shoulders completely and slowly shift your hips forward until you feel the balls of your feet taking your weight. Be careful not to move quickly, as this will often cause the heels to lift and the toes to grip the floor. Apply a downward pressure from the top of the knees down into the heels to help keep them on the floor.

The hands should rest on the floor beside or behind your feet with the fingers pointing forward. If the mobility of your hamstrings is limited and your hands don’t reach the floor easily, rest your palms on the front of your shinbones, with your legs straight. If the lower back is vulnerable to injury, take the feet hip-width apart, with your heels slightly wider than your big toes. Initially, don’t push with your arms to try to extend the spine. Let the movement of your inhalation into the back of your lungs create the subtle pressure to lift the weight of the spine softly, then surrender the weight of your spine on the exhalation. Notice the tendency for the hips to shift back and the weight to sink onto the heels with each cycle of breath. Constantly check to see how your weight is distributed and keep returning its force onto the balls of the feet.

As you begin to feel the subtle influence of the breath on the movement of the spine, notice the release of the exhalation, when the ribs are sinking and the diaphragm is soft. At this moment, flexible beginners whose hands reach the floor can extend from the top of the forearms, pressing into the palms, spread the shoulder blades, and elongate the spine from the back of the skull. The work of the arms should be in response to the movement in the spine—not the other way around. The intensity of the pose should build slowly from positioning and rhythmic breathing and never through excessive muscular force of the arms.

After holding the pose for five to 10 cycles of breath, slowly lift the spine on an inhalation, drawing the navel in slightly. If you’re coming up with tight buttocks and a gripped diaphragm, the lower back is vulnerable. Keep the buttocks and diaphragm passive, keep the legs straight, and allow the head to come up last, until you are standing in an upright position, arms resting at your sides.

Uttanasana, once mastered, allows for the understanding necessary for more advanced seated forward bends and beginning inversions. It helps build the digestive fire and, at the same time, is useful for rejuvenating the nervous system. With patient, persistent practice, Uttanasana will strengthen your mental focus and build your confidence as the confrontation found initially in the pose transforms into intelligence.

#8922. Post-Race Weight Gain: Why You’re Heavier After Finishing a Race (And Why It’s a Good Thing)

You wake up feeling sore and puffy the day after a race, step on the scale, and confirm what you intuitively feel: you’re a few pounds above your pre-race weight.

But why? Logically, a massive calorie burn (up to 10,000+ calories for an Ironman!) should tip the scale the other way, so something must be wrong.

Your first impulse may be to cut calories or jump right back into training. Please don’t! What you’re seeing is your body’s normal physiological response as it goes into full recovery mode.

Post-race weight gain isn’t the same as the off-season weight drift many athletes experience. That weight tends to build over months and is a separate conversation about energy balance. The jump you see on the scale in the first 24 to 72 hours after the race is mostly water. Specifically, your body is hard at work replenishing glycogen, rebuilding plasma volume, and retaining water and sodium as part of its hormonal stress-and-repair response. It’s most noticeable after a half or full iron-distance triathlon, where fueling, fluid intake, and stress load are highest.

Let’s dig into what’s going on, and why this temporary bump is actually a good sign.

Long-course races drain your muscle glycogen. As long as you eat plenty of carbs, your body starts refilling those stores within the first few hours after you finish. But the longer the race, the more muscle damage, which slows the process.

After a long-course race, full restoration can take several days, rather than the roughly 24 hours we see after shorter events. Here’s the kicker: each gram of newly synthesized glycogen is stored with approximately three grams of water. So, replenishing 400–500 grams of muscle glycogen adds about 3.5–4.5 pounds, mostly from water, packed in your muscles. In other words, much of the bump you see on the scale in the first few days is restored fuel.

Glycogen isn’t the only reason the scale climbs. It’s normal to finish a long race dehydrated, since even a solid race hydration strategy can’t fully offset hours of sweat losses. In the 24 to 72 hours after the race, fluid-conserving hormones (aldosterone and vasopressin) remain elevated, signaling your body to hold onto fluid to restore plasma volume and electrolyte balance. The extra water weight won’t stick around long, so don’t cut back on fluids or salt to bring the number down. Your body needs both right now.

Racing 70.3 or 140.6 miles puts your body under more stress than a typical training day. During and after the race, cortisol, your primary stress hormone, spikes, signaling your body to retain water. Prolonged physical exertion causes muscle microdamage and inflammation.

The longer, hotter, and tougher the race, the longer recovery may take. As your body begins repairs, fluid moves into damaged tissues, which can explain your tight, swollen legs. You’ll notice improvement when your kidneys start clearing the excess fluid, leading to more frequent bathroom visits. A little puffiness for a couple of days post-race means the repair process is underway.

As training volume comes down after a race, you might expect your appetite to follow. And, for the first several hours, it often does, since hard effort can temporarily suppress hunger. But over the next day or two, it returns with a vengeance. That’s because a slower-moving hormonal system (primarily ghrelin and leptin) signals your brain to respond to the energy deficit you built up on race day.

You may feel hungrier for several days, often craving energy-dense, salty, carb-rich foods (think fries, burgers, and pizza). And all that yummy food, along with the water and sodium that come with it, adds to the scale number too. It’s not a lack of willpower or a total loss of control; it’s your body refueling.

Following an endurance race, some swelling is expected, but I’d be remiss not to flag a few scenarios that, although rare, require medical attention.

If one leg swells, especially with calf pain, warmth, or redness, it may indicate a blood clot. Swelling with shortness of breath or chest pain is an emergency; seek immediate attention.

Dark cola-colored urine with severe muscle pain or weakness could signal rhabdomyolysis: a condition involving severe muscle breakdown that can lead to kidney damage.

And if you finish the race heavier than you started and experience confusion, headache, or nausea, it could be hyponatremia (low blood sodium); seek medical help right away.

For most athletes, a few extra pounds in the days after a long-distance race signals a healthy recovery. Still, it can be tempting, especially if you keep close tabs on your weight, to see the number go up and immediately want to cut back or restrict.

Resist the urge. Your body needs carbohydrates and protein to rebuild glycogen and repair tissue; your fluid and electrolyte balance needs restoring, and your immune system needs adequate energy while under duress. Restricting food and fluids now won’t get your weight back on track. It will delay glycogen restoration, prolong fatigue and soreness, and potentially increase your risk of illness.

As your fluid levels normalize and inflammation subsides, most of the extra weight comes off naturally, typically within three to seven days. You’ve demanded a lot from your body in training and on race day, so give it what it needs: plenty of nutrient-rich food, adequate hydration, rest, and quality sleep. Then step back and trust your body and the process.

The most widely cited framework for income classes comes from the Pew Research Center, which uses a straightforward formula based on the national median household income. Pew defines three tiers:

Using the most recent Census Bureau data with a national median household income of approximately $84,900, the thresholds for a three-person household look like this:

The "upper middle class" label is not an official Pew category — it is a colloquial term most commonly used to describe the band between the middle of the middle class and the beginning of the upper class. Think of it as the top quarter of the middle-income range through the entry point of the upper-income range: households earning roughly $106,000 to $169,800.

These definitions are adjusted for household size using an equivalence scale. A single person needs less income than a family of five to achieve the same standard of living. Pew adjusts all income figures to a three-person household equivalent, which is why the thresholds you see in different sources sometimes vary — they may be using different household sizes as their reference point.

National income thresholds are useful starting points, but they obscure a critical reality: the cost of living varies so dramatically across the United States that the same income places you in different classes depending on where you live. Pew Research's cost-of-living adjusted data reveals just how stark these differences are.

A household earning $150,000 in Jackson, Mississippi — where the cost of living is roughly 83% of the national average — has purchasing power equivalent to about $180,700 nationally. That same $150,000 in San Francisco, where costs run about 180% of the national average, has purchasing power equivalent to only $83,300 — technically middle class by Pew's national definitions.

This explains why so many households earning $150,000 to $200,000 in coastal cities feel middle class despite technically being upper-income by national standards. They are not wrong — their lived experience of housing costs, childcare, and taxes genuinely consumes their income at the same rate as middle-income households in lower-cost areas.

Income class and wealth class are not the same thing. The Federal Reserve's Survey of Consumer Finances reveals that high income does not automatically translate to high net worth. Many upper-income households carry large mortgages, student loans, and car payments that consume much of their earnings. Meanwhile, some middle-income households with high savings rates accumulate substantial wealth over time.

The FI community lives in this gap. A household earning $90,000 that saves 50% of their income and invests consistently will have a higher net worth within 10-15 years than a household earning $250,000 that saves 5%. Income determines your ceiling; savings rate determines your trajectory. This is why ChooseFI focuses on savings rate and investable net worth as the primary metrics of financial progress — not income class labels.

The financial independence community occupies a unique position in the income class framework. Survey data from FIRE-focused communities suggests the median household income among FI seekers is roughly $130,000 to $160,000 — placing most in the upper-middle-class to lower-upper-income range. However, successful FI stories span the entire income spectrum, from teachers earning $55,000 to tech executives earning $500,000.

What distinguishes FI community members from their income peers is not what they earn but what they keep. While the average upper-middle-class household saves 8-12% of income, FI-path households in the same income range typically save 40-60%. This results in net worth accumulation that dramatically outpaces their income class peers.

The lesson from this comparison is that income class labels describe your earning power, but they say nothing about your financial trajectory. A middle-income household on the FI path will typically surpass the net worth of upper-income households who spend freely. The FI framework redefines "class" around financial freedom rather than consumption — your class is determined not by what you can afford to buy, but by how many years of expenses your investments can cover.

Income class definitions use household income, which combines the earnings of all adults in a home. This creates a nuance worth understanding: a dual-income household where each partner earns $75,000 has the same household income ($150,000) as a single-earner household at that level, but the dual-income household often faces higher total costs (two commutes, potentially more childcare) and different tax treatment. When evaluating where you fall, always use your total household income before taxes and compare to thresholds adjusted for your household size.

The distinction between wealth and income is the foundation of financial independence. Your income class describes your present earning power. Your net worth describes your accumulated financial freedom. The FI community's central insight is that you can move from any income class to financial independence by controlling the gap between what you earn and what you spend — and investing the difference consistently in low-cost index funds over time.

Free calculators, a personalized FI roadmap, and a community of 25K+ on the same journey.

Whether you are middle class, upper middle class, or upper class by any definition, your path to financial independence depends on one number: your savings rate. A middle-income household saving 50% of their income will reach FI decades before an upper-income household saving 5%. Focus on growing the gap between what you earn and what you spend — the class label takes care of itself.

Add up all pre-tax income for your household — wages, self-employment, investment income, and any other sources. Compare to the Pew thresholds adjusted for your household size. For a three-person household, middle income is $56,600 to $169,800.

Use a cost-of-living calculator to adjust your income to the national equivalent. A $120,000 income in a city with 130% cost-of-living has the same purchasing power as $92,300 nationally. This adjusted number is a more honest reflection of your class position.

Your net worth — assets minus liabilities — is a better indicator of financial health than income alone. The median net worth for upper-middle-class households is roughly $465,000. If you are above that with a lower income, you are wealthier than your income class suggests.

Divide your annual savings (including employer retirement contributions) by your gross income. The national average is under 5%. The FI community targets 40-60%. Your savings rate is the single most important predictor of when you will reach financial independence.

Multiply your annual spending by 25 to find your FI number (based on the 4% safe withdrawal rate). Then use your current savings rate and existing net worth to estimate how many years until you reach that number. This timeline matters more than any income class label.

According to Pew Research, upper-income households earn more than double the national median household income. For a three-person household in 2026, that threshold is approximately $169,800. However, this varies significantly by location — in San Francisco, you would need roughly $306,000 to have the same purchasing power as $169,800 nationally.

Upper middle class generally describes households in the top 20-30% of earners but below the top 5% — roughly $106,000 to $169,800 for a three-person household. Upper class typically refers to households above $169,800 (top 19%). The top 5% begins at roughly $280,000 and the top 1% at approximately $590,000. These are income-based definitions and do not account for net worth.

By national standards, $200,000 household income places you in the upper-income category (above the $169,800 threshold for a three-person household). However, in high-cost cities like San Francisco, New York, or Boston, $200,000 has purchasing power equivalent to roughly $111,000 to $130,000 nationally — solidly middle class in terms of lived experience.

The Federal Reserve Survey of Consumer Finances shows the median net worth of upper-income households is approximately $805,400. The top 10% of U.S. households by net worth have $1.9 million or more, and the top 1% have $11.1 million or more. Net worth is a more meaningful measure of financial security than income because it reflects accumulated wealth, not just current earning power.

Lifestyle inflation is the primary reason. Many households increase their spending in lockstep with income increases — larger homes, newer cars, private schools, premium vacations — leaving little margin for savings. A household earning $300,000 that spends $290,000 accumulates wealth more slowly than one earning $100,000 that spends $50,000. The FI community calls this the HENRY problem: High Earner, Not Rich Yet.

Pew Research adjusts income thresholds using an equivalence scale based on household size. A single person needs roughly $56,600 to be middle income (the lower bound), while a family of five needs roughly $126,500 for the same standard of living. Larger households need more income to achieve the same class designation because they have more people sharing the resources.

Income class labels provide useful context for understanding where you stand relative to other American households, but they are a poor measure of financial health. Plenty of upper-income households are one job loss away from financial crisis because they spend everything they earn, while many middle-income households on the FI path have built net worth that places them in the top 10% of all Americans. The framework that matters most is not whether you are middle class, upper middle class, or upper class — it is whether the gap between your income and your spending is large enough to build financial independence within a timeline that matters to you. Focus on three numbers: your savings rate, your investable net worth, and your FI number. Everything else is a label that describes your present circumstances, not your financial future.

#8917. Camel Pose Helps Build Balance, Strength, and Flexibility

In Yoga Journal’s Archives series, we share a curated collection of articles originally published in past issues beginning in 1975. This article about Camel Pose first appeared in the September-October 2001 issue of Yoga Journal. You can find more of our Archives here.

When looking at the meanings of the names of yoga asanas, especially those named after animals, you can find clues—sometimes literal and other times only suggestive —about the nature of the pose. With Camel Pose (Ustrasana) it’s a little of both.

What was it about this pose that inspired yogis of ages past to name it after the camel? Only by strenuously stretching the imagination can we find any resemblance to a healthy backbend in the shape of this animal.

Anatomically a camel’s body appears to be an assemblage of odd, unrelated parts, and the hump—the most unique and obvious characteristic—looks almost like an afterthought. Although camel humps may appear to be part of the spine, they are actually sacks of fat used to store partially digested food for long journeys. Through centuries of Asian and African civilization, the camel has also had a reputation for being a stubborn, ill-tempered animal with a serious lack of intelligence. Since it’s doubtful that the ancient yogis aspired to the image of lifting the spine like a camel hump, and a camel’s temperament is not exactly something to emulate in one’s yoga practice, why is this posed called the “camel”?

Traditionally the camel’s presence in the desert, one of the most inhospitable environments on our planet, has been one of the primary forces sustaining human life there. Though a camel’s eyesight is not keen, it relies on some inner compass to navigate its way through the desert. Used primarily as pack animals, camels instinctively know if a load is too heavy to endure over a long journey or if the weight is improperly balanced —and will refuse to move until the load is adjusted. Without a road map, in constantly changing surroundings of drifting sands, camels have the ability to read the signs and find the oases of green where water is present and food at hand.

Looking at the Camel Pose, we can begin to see a parallel. For many beginners, the “environment” in backbends is equally inhospitable. In general, beginning to bend backward is difficult and sometimes frightening, yet backbends are essential to maintaining a healthy spine. Generally we function in a forward-facing, right-side-up world, relying heavily on our eyes for our sense of identity and direction. In Camel, we must learn to cultivate another way of seeing. The shape of the pose places the head and one’s vision behind the body. It is an alien experience; our view of the world is literally turned upside down.

Our normal context for relating to ourselves and the image that sustains us is lost. For the beginner, a common reaction to the fear that comes from this loss of context is to shorten or hold the breath.

In addition, beginners often habitually contract the muscles of the buttocks and abdomen. The neck, if weak, becomes vulnerable as the shoulders grip for protection. When these reactions are present in the body, the movement in this pose does not respond well, especially if the student uses excessive muscular force. The pose feels out of balance, and the more we struggle, the less the pose responds. This only deepens the frustration, and we are likely to shut down or check out.

Basically there are two techniques for entering Camel Pose safely: dropping in from an upright kneeling position or lifting up from a seated position. Once you master these approaches in Camel Pose, a foundation has been laid for approaching the more advanced backbend Wheel Pose (Urdhva Dhanurasana) either by lifting up from the floor or by dropping back from a standing position.

I recommend dropping in from the kneeling position in Camel for your first attempt if your lower back or knees are sensitive. This approach also works with gravity to help you avoid the natural tendencies of the beginner to overdo muscular effort. Begin by kneeling on your mat with your torso upright and the thighs perpendicular to the floor. Place your legs hip-width apart, with the tops of the feet flat on the floor and your arms at your sides. If your lower back is weak, place your hands on your buttocks to give more support to the lumbar spine as you enter the pose. Let your shoulders hang from the sides of your neck and drop your collarbones away from your ears. Initially keep your head upright, with your chin drawn slightly in toward the center of the throat. As you inhale, feel the fullness of your breath feeding the back, rather than the chest.

With each exhalation, let the weight of your chest and abdominal organs sink, as you keep the spine engaged upward from the back of the skull. Visualize the energy of the pose looping down along the front of the body (from the chest down through the hips to the shinbones on the floor) and up along the back of the body (through the spine to the crown of the head). Slowly take your head back; keep the throat soft and the shoulders down and slightly forward, with the shoulder blades broad. Avoid hardening the buttocks or the abdomen. Keep the top of the hips pressing firmly down into the knees, and as you bend the spine backward, let your arms hang from your shoulders with your fingers reaching back to touch the heels.

If the stress is excessive in your lower back, inhale back to an upright position, and after resting for a moment, try the pose again. Once your hands reach your feet, maintain the downward pressure from the top of the hip bones pressing into the knees, continue releasing the chest and abdomen down, and feel the lift from the floor into the thoracic spine.

The head should hang freely, with the neck supported by the width of the trapezius muscle along the top of the shoulders. The breath should remain slow and rhythmic, and with each exhalation, the release of the frontal body will propel the lift in the back body. After three or four cycles of breath, inhale back to an upright position.

Lifting up from the seated position can be more accessible when the neck is weak, but it tends to stress the legs and knees more intensely than the first approach, due to the fact that you are working against gravity. If your knees are weak, take care not to overstress them. And be patient—if your knees and groins are tight, you may not achieve full extension in the pose at first.

From an upright kneeling position, sit between your heels (use a block between your feet if necessary, with the palms of your hands placed on your heels, fingers pointing back. Slowly lean back, straightening your arms, taking your weight onto your hands, and lift your hips upward.

Press the shoulders forward, broaden the shoulder blades, and let the neck rest in the trapezius muscle as you take the head slowly back. As the hips lift upward and more weight is taken onto the lower legs, press the tops of the hip bones (ilia) down into the knees and lift the spine. Be careful to keep the abdomen and buttocks soft and the energy of the chest dropping.

Once you are in the pose, the release of the frontal body will propel the lift in the back body. After three or four cycles of breath, slowly lower your hips on an inhalation and return to the seated position. With Camel Pose, you begin to develop balance and strength in the spine, promoting flexibility in the shoulders and suppleness in the abdomen. By relying less on outer sight for your sense of identity and position in the world, you can cultivate an inner vision that expands into your more authentic, intuitive self.
