#8865. How to Strengthen Your Arms and Wrists With Upward Plank Variations

In Yoga Journal’s Archives series, we share a curated collection of articles originally published in past issues beginning in 1975. This article about Upward Plank Pose variations first appeared in the June 2007 issue of Yoga Journal. Find more of our Archives here.

What direction do you face when you practice yoga? Probably whichever way your usual practice space dictates. But the old yogis were very clear that we should face either east or north when practicing, per the classical yoga text the Gheranda Samhita 5.48. Why?

Yoga scholar Alain Danielou writes that the four cardinal and four intermediate points of the compass have special significance. The thunderbolt-wielding Indra, lord of all the protectors and prototype of courage and power in Hindu mythology, guards the east.

By facing in a certain direction when we practice, we acknowledge and draw on energetic properties for support and inspiration. So again, why east and north? East is the quarter of the rising sun, which Hindus revere as the “breath of creatures” or the source of all earthly life.

The sun represents the embodied Self, its dawn the emergence of the “light” of spiritual self-awareness and insight. North is the quarter of the pole star, called dhruva (pronounced DREW-vah) in Sanskrit, meaning “fixed, eternal.” Its constancy amid the ever-wheeling night sky is considered the embodiment of willpower, certainly a quality all serious yogis covet. In India too, north is the realm of the majestic Himalayas, where Hindu tradition places the mythic mountain Meru, thought of as the “navel” of the earth as well as the bridge to the celestial world of the gods and goddesses.

What compass directions would you assign to the back and front of your body? According to the yogis, your back body is the west, your front body the east. In Sanskrit, paschima means both “back” and “west,” while purva means both “front” and “east.” So this terminology gives us the names of two common and related poses: Paschimottanasana (Intense Stretch of the West Pose or, more commonly, Seated Forward Bend), which stretches your back body, and Purvottanasana (Intense Stretch of the East or Upward Plank Pose)—pictured here—a slight backbend and front-body stretch that provides a nice counterpose to its western opposite.

Purvottanasana stretches you all the way from your ankles through the thighs, groins, and belly, up to the shoulders and throat. It also strengthens your wrists and the muscles on the backs of the upper arms (triceps) and firms the buttocks—which, if you believe popular media claims, is a primary benefit of yoga. It will also help improve your sense of balance and calm. And it’s a great counterpose to the commonly practiced Chaturanga Dandasana (Four-Limbed Staff Pose).

If you have serious wrist, shoulder, or neck problems, practice this pose only under the guidance of an experienced teacher. You’ll need a chair, a block, and a wall to practice some of these preparatory poses.

Sit on the floor with your legs extended straight in front of you in Dandasana (Staff Pose). Rotate your thighs inward, big toes in, heels out, and press your palms to the floor slightly behind your buttocks with your fingers pointing forward toward your feet. If your shoulders protest, you can turn your fingers outward.

Bend your elbows and sink or hollow your front torso, spreading your scapulas as far away from your spine as possible. Rotate your upper arms inward and widen your elbows, letting the heads of your upper arm bones (humeri) jut forward. Enjoy the stretch between the scapulas for a minute or so.

Then straighten your elbows and lift your chest while leaving your lower body on the floor. Often, students simply squeeze their scapulas together and shove their lower front ribs forward, which hardens the front torso, restricting the free flow of breath, and compresses the low back. Instead, keep your scapulas wide and front torso soft.

Press the bases of your index fingers into the floor and hug your triceps against your humeri. As your elbows straighten out and your chest lifts, maintain the inward rotation of your upper arms, which will help the scapulas stay broad. Release your head back slightly, but don’t fully extend the neck. Trace the stretch along your front torso from your pubis to your sternum (breastbone).

Imagine directing your inhalations into the space behind your sternum (“imagine” because there’s no lung there, just your heart), increasing the lift of your chest. With each exhalation, reaffirm the opposing movements of the inner hands (down against the floor) and scapulas (up against your back). Hold for a minute or two. Repeat two or three times, until you feel confident you’ll be able to recreate the inward rotation of the thighs and arms and the actions of the hands and scapulas while maintaining the soft front torso when called on to do so in the more challenging circumstances of the full pose.

Next, sit on the front edge of a chair with your knees bent, heels directly below your knees. Wrap your hands around the back edge of the seat (for this first part of the exercise your upper arms will naturally rotate outward), thumbs pointing outward (Figure 1).

Inhale and slowly lift your buttocks away from the seat until your thighs, torso, and head form one long diagonal line, with your arms more or less perpendicular to the chair seat. Rotate your thighs slightly inward, and push (but don’t physically move) your knees away from your torso. The thigh rotation will tend to make your tailbone sag toward the floor, collapsing your belly, so firm your tailbone against your back pelvis and lengthen it. Hold this position for a minute, then sit back on the chair. On an inhalation, release the back edge of the seat and return to sitting upright. Take a few breaths.

If you like, repeat this exercise with your fingers turned forward, palms on the seat, and your upper arms rotated inward. Hold for one minute, release on an exhalation, and rest.

If you want to take this exercise to its limit, lift your buttocks again and extend your legs. Do your right leg first. Inhale and press out through your heel to straighten your knee, but suspend your foot a few inches off the floor. Then rotate your thigh inward, point your toes, and bring your sole to the floor. Just as the bases of your index forgers press the seat, so the base of your big toe presses on the floor. Repeat with the left leg. Once again, hold for a minute and release on an exhalation.

If you want to continue, brace the back legs of a chair against the wall and lay your block on the seat (if you’re using a wood block, cover the seat with a sticky mat to keep the block from sliding). Set the block on either its lowest or middle height near the front edge of the seat.

Sit on the floor right in front of the chair, knees bent, feet on the floor, heels 12 to 15 inches away from your buttocks, and lean back against the front edge of the seat. Press your hands on the floor with your fingers turned either forward, to the sides, or back—you choose—just in front of the feet of the chair legs.

Inhale and do what you did for the first part of the first exercise: Lift your thighs and torso parallel to the floor (heels below the knees), and then release your head back onto the block to take any pressure off your neck. If the block is too high or too low, come down and readjust. If you are having trouble opening your chest, it may help to reinforce the firmness of your palms against the floor, your scapulas against your back, and your triceps against the humeri. Then again, it may not.

Don’t get discouraged. Just practice this exercise every other day or so for the next few weeks, and you’ll be surprised how quickly things improve. Whatever happens, hold the pose for 30 seconds to a minute, then release to the floor on an exhalation. Smile.

If you can’t boost your chest, though, trying to extend your legs will probably make matters worse, so I don’t recommend it. But if your chest is reasonably lifted, then it’s acceptable to extend your legs.

Having trouble getting the balls of your feet, especially the bases of your big toes, on the floor? Position a rolled-up sticky mat on the floor where the balls of your feet will be when your legs are extended and press against that.

Feeling frustrated on a Monday morning is not a reason to quit. But persistent patterns that affect your health, relationships, and long-term career growth are legitimate signals worth examining. The challenge is separating temporary frustration from genuine misalignment.

The FI community approaches this differently from mainstream career advice. Instead of asking "Am I happy at work?" — which fluctuates daily — we ask: "Is this role aligned with my long-term financial and personal goals?" That reframe turns an emotional decision into a strategic one.

Before you submit your resignation, your finances need to be ready regardless of how miserable you are. Quitting without financial preparation trades one source of stress for another.

The FI community has a massive advantage here. If you have been building toward financial independence — even if you are not there yet — your savings provide a runway that most people do not have. A $200,000 investment portfolio at a 4% safe withdrawal rate provides $8,000 per year in sustainable income, which dramatically reduces the pressure of a job search.

The worst time to make a career decision is when you are emotionally overwhelmed. A terrible meeting, a passed-over promotion, or a toxic interaction with a coworker can make quitting feel urgent when the situation may actually be temporary or fixable.

Use the 30-day test: if you have wanted to quit for fewer than 30 consecutive days, it is likely a temporary frustration. If the feeling has persisted — or intensified — for 30+ days, it is a pattern worth taking seriously.

How you leave a job matters as much as why you leave. Your professional reputation follows you for your entire career, and the people you work with today may be the hiring managers, clients, or references of tomorrow.

Two weeks notice: This is the minimum professional standard in the United States. For senior roles, three to four weeks is more appropriate. Check your employment contract — some roles require 30, 60, or 90 days notice.

The resignation conversation: Schedule a private meeting with your direct manager. Keep it brief and positive. Say: "I have decided to move on to a new opportunity. I want to thank you for [specific positive thing], and I am committed to making the transition as smooth as possible. My last day would be [date]."

The transition plan: Document your ongoing projects, key contacts, passwords, and processes. Offer to train your replacement. Complete as much outstanding work as possible. A strong exit creates goodwill that pays dividends for years.

What not to do: Do not badmouth the company, your boss, or your coworkers — not in the resignation meeting, not in your exit interview, not on social media. Even if your grievances are legitimate, airing them publicly hurts your reputation more than theirs.

Conventional advice says never quit without another job lined up. The FI community takes a more nuanced view: it depends on your financial position and the severity of the situation.

If you are leaving due to company changes — layoffs, restructuring, or role elimination — negotiate your severance package. Many employees accept the first offer without realizing severance is negotiable. Key leverage points include your tenure, difficulty of replacement, willingness to sign a non-compete or non-disparagement clause, and any outstanding commissions or bonuses.

Common severance components to negotiate: extended pay (push for 2-4 weeks per year of tenure), continued health insurance coverage, outplacement services, vesting acceleration for equity, and a positive reference commitment.

Health insurance is often the biggest financial concern when leaving a job. You have two primary options:

COBRA: Continues your employer plan for up to 18 months. You pay the full premium (your share plus what your employer was paying) plus a 2% administrative fee. COBRA typically costs $500-$700 per month for individual coverage and $1,400-$2,000+ for family coverage. It is expensive but familiar.

ACA Marketplace: Depending on your income after leaving, you may qualify for substantial subsidies. If your annual income drops below 400% of the federal poverty level, premium tax credits can reduce your monthly cost to $100-$400 for comprehensive coverage. FI seekers who leave jobs often qualify for significant subsidies because their earned income drops even if their net worth is high — ACA subsidies are based on income, not wealth.

Here is where financial independence changes everything. When you have significant savings — even if you have not reached full FI — you have leverage that most employees lack. You can negotiate from strength, take career risks, and walk away from toxic situations without financial desperation.

A $500,000 portfolio at a 4% withdrawal rate provides $20,000 per year indefinitely. That is not enough to live on for most people, but combined with a working spouse, reduced expenses, or part-time work, it transforms "should I quit my job" from a terrifying question into a strategic calculation. FI is not just about never working again — it is about having the financial security to make career decisions based on alignment and purpose rather than desperation and fear.

Free calculators, a personalized FI roadmap, and a community of 25K+ on the same journey.

The FI community has a saying: financial independence is not about quitting your job — it is about having the freedom to choose whether to keep it. Every dollar you save and invest is a vote for your future autonomy. When you have 12-24 months of expenses saved, you negotiate from strength. When you reach Coast FI or beyond, a bad job becomes a choice, not a trap. Build your FI runway and the question changes from "Can I afford to quit?" to "Does this role still serve my goals?"

Work through these steps before making your decision.

Have you consistently wanted to leave for 30+ days? If no, wait. Temporary frustration is not a reason to upend your career. If yes, proceed to step two.

Pro tip: Keep a brief daily journal noting your satisfaction level 1-10. Data beats feelings for decision-making.

Is the issue your boss, your role, your compensation, the culture, or the industry? Some problems follow you to the next job. A bad manager is fixable by transferring. An industry you hate requires a bigger change.

Verify your emergency fund, health insurance options, debt situation, and FI runway. If you are not financially ready, keep working while you build your safety net and search for alternatives.

Before quitting, have you requested a transfer, a raise, a role change, or a conversation with HR? Many solvable problems go unaddressed because employees assume the answer will be no.

Pro tip: A direct conversation with your manager about your concerns resolves the issue 40% of the time.

If you decide to leave, secure your next opportunity (if possible), give appropriate notice, document your work for your successor, and maintain every professional relationship.

Pro tip: Never burn bridges. The colleague you leave today may be the hiring manager at your dream company in three years.

At minimum, 3-6 months of essential expenses in a liquid savings account. If you are quitting without another job lined up, aim for 6-12 months. The FI community recommends having your emergency fund fully funded, health insurance secured, and ideally some progress toward financial independence to provide a psychological safety net.

If your job is causing persistent anxiety, depression, or physical health symptoms that do not improve with coping strategies, therapy, or workplace changes — yes, your health must come first. But do it strategically: secure health insurance, build your financial runway, and consult a therapist or career coach before making the leap. Never make a permanent career decision during a temporary emotional crisis.

Generally, quitting gives you more control over the narrative, timing, and terms. Being fired can qualify you for unemployment benefits (quitting usually does not), but it can also create a negative reference. If you sense a termination is coming, consider whether negotiating a mutual separation with severance is an option. Document everything and consult an employment attorney if you believe the termination may be discriminatory or retaliatory.

Be honest and frame it positively. Acceptable explanations include: career transition (took time to retrain or earn a certification), personal development (traveled, volunteered, or cared for family), or strategic job search (took time to find the right fit rather than settling). Employers increasingly accept career gaps — especially post-2020 — as long as you can articulate what you did during the time off.

COBRA (Consolidated Omnibus Budget Reconciliation Act) lets you continue your employer health plan for up to 18 months after leaving. You pay the full premium (your share plus what your employer contributed) plus a 2% admin fee. Individual coverage typically costs $500-$700/month and family coverage runs $1,400-$2,000+/month. The ACA marketplace is often cheaper, especially if your income drops after leaving.

FI savings transform the equation entirely. With a substantial portfolio, you have a financial runway that removes the urgency and desperation from the decision. Even partial FI — having 2-5 years of expenses invested — means you can quit a toxic job, take time to find the right next role, or transition to lower-paying but more fulfilling work. FI is not just about retiring early; it is about having the leverage to make career decisions from a position of strength rather than fear.

The question "should I quit my job?" deserves a framework, not an impulse. Apply the 30-day test, diagnose the real problem, verify your financial readiness, explore internal solutions, and then make a deliberate decision. If you have been building toward financial independence, your savings give you something most people lack: the freedom to walk away from a bad situation without financial panic. FI is the ultimate career insurance — it turns "I have to stay" into "I choose to stay or go." Build your runway, protect your reputation, and make the decision from a position of strength.

#8861. I Used to Buy Cycling Kit for How It Looked. Now I Buy It for How It Gets Me Through the Ride—My Three Rules for Cycling Kit

Versatility, comfort, and durability matter most when choosing kit that improves your ride.

Gear-obsessed editors choose every product we review. We may earn commission if you buy from a link. How we test gear.

After spending almost two decades riding and years running bike shops, I have narrowed down my priorities for key criteria when buying cycling apparel. I’m looking for a product that is durable, performs well in varying conditions, and is comfortable over miles on the bike.

Apparel falls into different categories depending on the rider. For some, it falls into a category of fashion. Those riders want their choice of apparel to tell a story about who they are on the bike.

For other riders, safety is the biggest driving factor. This group is intentionally easy to see by their bright colors riding by. While other riders solely look for a great deal, digging through clearance racks at bike shops as the seasons change.

Finding kit that performs the way we want our bike to perform can give us a better experience on our ride compared to getting whatever the cool kids are wearing—just for fashion’s sake. Here I’m going to dive deeper into each of the priorities I have for my jerseys and bibs to shed some light on why there’s value in this shift—especially this time of year.

What I look for in a jersey, especially for fall, is one that will vent well on the way up, but keep me comfortable on the way back down. I love a good gilet, especially leaving it open on the way down a road. If my jersey can do what the gilet does then that’s one less piece of kit I have to buy and bring. Lately I’ve been using the Dottore Hybrid Long Sleeve jersey from Q36.5 and it checks off all those boxes.

I tried this jersey out on a recent trip to Italy where we had a roughly 2,500-foot climb followed immediately by an equal descent. The temperature was hovering around the mid-fifties and usually, I would bring a vest for a ride like this. However, I was told this jersey should be perfect for these conditions, so I wanted to give it a proper test. On the way up I didn’t feel a need to unzip the jersey at all and on the screaming descent I never felt cold. Somehow Q36.5 figured out how to give the best of both worlds in one jersey.

Many of us think of a good pair of bibs being the key component to comfort on the bike—and in some ways that’s not wrong. Comfort on your sit bones can be greatly improved by getting the right saddle and sometimes a bike fit to determine what that saddle is and how the saddle should be positioned. But a good pair of bibs can still greatly improve comfort on the bike even after you get a fit and get the right saddle.

Not all chamois pads are created equal, and not all bibs hold the chamois in the place you need after miles of pedaling. Part of the challenge with bibs is you don’t really know until you get on the bike to ride—and good bibs aren’t exactly an inexpensive purchase.

“An unlined full length bib like the Velocio Luxe Tights offers a more comfortable go to bib for when you need to cover you legs but don't need to have fleece warmth,” says Trevor Raab, our resident bike racer and photographer at Bicycling. What I typically look for in bibs is a pair with minimal seams, has a chamois pad that offers both padding and ventilation, and good support and structure from the overalls to help hold the bib in place.

The final piece of my puzzle for gear and apparel is durability. Part of the reality is that just like bikes, apparel has pieces that are more consumable than others and will need to be replaced over time.

I’m someone who tends to stress test both bikes and apparel from hitting the ground. I haven’t found any apparel that holds up to a good impact to the pavement or gravel— as can be seen by many of my bibs having a tear on one of the hips. However, not all material holds up the same over time.

From the bibs that I have tried I either haven’t put enough miles in them or I have put over a year of miles on them and there is a noticeable impact to the comfort of the chamois. But something to note: more padding isn’t inherently better in a chamois. From a durability perspective and my experience, the thicker pads compress over time and aren’t necessarily more comfortable on the bike. The pair I’ve gotten the most miles on this year are the Q36.5 Dottore Bib Shorts. I’ve put a few hundred miles in them and they are still as comfortable as the first ride. Every rider I talk to that has tried this pair of bibs has experienced the same thing.

It’s important to acknowledge the pricing of some of this high-end kit is not a small investment. Shifting your perspective of apparel as just clothes to looking at apparel as gear can make it easier to understand. Too many times when I worked in a shop someone would spend thousands of dollars on a bike only to buy low-priced apparel. There’s nothing wrong with buying entry-level kit to get started. But if you are someone who spends thousands on your bike, then it’s likely ride quality matters to you regardless of the price. If you start to think about your apparel as gear, it’s easier to see that great apparel can impact your ride just like riding on a great bike.

Jason Griffin is Bicycling's Senior Health and Fitness Editor, bringing more than a decade of fitness experience and years in the cycling industry to every story. A former personal trainer and bike shop manager, he's lined up for crits, tackled enduros, but prefers getting lost on multi-day bikepacking adventures. Lately though, his toughest balancing act has been fitting trainer rides between family life and the next adventure.

#8858. Inside an Elite Running Group’s Marathon Training Strategies That Get Them to the Front of the Pack

Go inside the Boulder-based team helping Hellen Obiri, Joe Klecker, and others chase NYC success, and learn how their approach can improve your own training.

Six years ago, when Joe Klecker was named to the inaugural class of the On Athletics Club (OAC) in Boulder, Colorado, his goals were all about racing fast on the track. But based on his physiology, his tenacity, and even his genes, coach Dathan Ritzenhein already knew Klecker was destined to become a marathoner—and probably a very good one.

When the team now known as OAC Global formed in the summer of 2020, it featured eight postcollegiate runners chasing Olympic berths from 1,500 to 10,000 meters. The OAC sent several runners (including Klecker) to the Tokyo Olympics and brought home medals from Paris.

But track success was only the first step of what Ritzenhein envisioned. In the years since, he and coach Laura Thweatt have built an elite marathon program, too.

Kenyan great Hellen Obiri, four-time Major Marathon winner and current women’s New York City Marathon course record holder, put OAC on the marathon map after joining in 2022. The progression of Klecker (with a marathon PR of 2:05:56 from Boston), along with newer teammates Ryan Ford (2:05:46 marathon PR) and Patrick Kiprop (59:14 half marathon PR), has helped to solidify the team’s presence on the roads.

As all four prepare for the NYC Marathon, we went behind the curtain at the OAC Global Training Facility in Boulder to learn what has fueled their success.

When On recruited Obiri to Boulder in 2022, the two-time Olympic silver medalist at 5,000 meters was about to move up to the marathon. That meant shifting from pure track speed and relatively low mileage (80 miles per week) to 120- to 125-mile weeks and grinding sessions like 25K tempo runs.

With no other marathoners on the team, she did portions of her long runs with 10,000-meter runner Alicia Monson and some longer tempo efforts and fartleks with Klecker. All three benefited.

Obiri became one of the best marathoners in the world, winning New York and Boston twice and an Olympic bronze medal in Paris; Monson broke the American 5,000- and 10,000-meter records in 2023, and Klecker got a taste of what marathon training was all about, which gave him proper perspective as he was about to begin his first marathon build.

“[Obiri’s] level is so high that, on a lot of our long runs and even some fartleks, we would overlap for a good chunk of those workouts,” Klecker, 29, tells Runner’s World. “And for me, it was harder than I thought. When you’re racing on the track, a long run is kind of a chill day because all of your hard work is on the track. But when you’d see her go out and do her long runs, she was just hammering from the start, and so I knew I really had to wrap my head around this new way of training for the roads.”

As Klecker got closer to his marathon debut last fall, the OAC signed Ford as his primary training partner. They developed a synergy, but weren’t entirely aligned in their schedules because Ford was building up to the Chicago Marathon and Klecker was preparing for New York a month later. But they did sync up for all of their training (including harder workouts) as they prepared for Boston, and that paid off with better racing execution and significant time drops.

The team recently added an even faster teammate in Kiprop, a 25-year-old Kenyan and former University of Arkansas star, after big wins at the Lilac Bloomsday 12K and Peachtree Road Race 10K. He ran 59:14 in his half marathon debut in January in Houston and moved to Boulder in early August to join Klecker and Ford at the start of the 12-week New York buildup.

Klecker admits his marathon debut was mostly about surviving 26 miles. He trained to run a measured race holding 5:00 pace the whole way. That meant he fell off the lead pack when surging began along First Avenue, but his strength allowed him to reel in runners who were fading in the final miles.

This year, the trio of Klecker, Ford, and Kiprop have been able to push each other on hard long runs and marathon-specific workouts aimed at mimicking the surges and inconsistent pacing at the front of the pack in New York City.

“This year, the goal is to be up front and try to race for that podium and not just catch the people who die. You can’t do that from two minutes back late in the race,” Klecker says. “Now, based on the training we’ve done through a natural progression of workouts, it feels I should be ready to go with some moves. That's kind of been the whole focus of the past year, to be more competitive throughout the race.”

Training with the team has worked well for Obiri, 36, who is coming off a personal best 2:15:53 runner-up effort at the London Marathon in April. But at times, she has had a penchant to run too hard in training with faster teammates, which is why OAC has recruited seasonal training partners closer to her pace from Kenya over the past two years. (This year, it is Dennis Kipkosgeu, a 2:13 marathoner.)

She heads to New York as the defending champion after what she considers her best buildup yet.

“The growth of our road running team feels amazing because I have runners to train with every day,” she says of the OAC team. “When I joined in 2022, I was the only marathoner, and that was hard. This gives me confidence because there are four of us working so hard together.”

By early 2025, Ritzenhein wanted a coach to lead the road program day to day while he and assistant coach Kelsey Quinn stayed focused on the track group that included Yared Nuguse, bronze medalist in the 1500 at the Paris Olympics.

Thweatt, a longtime Boulder runner, had just retired from her own pro career and posted on Instagram that she was looking for new opportunities. Two days later, Ritzenhein called her. Within about two weeks, she was the OAC’s marathon coach.

A 2:25:38 marathoner who twice finished fifth at the U.S. Olympic Trials (in the marathon in 2020 and 10,000 meters in 2016) and notched top-10 finishes in London and New York, Thweatt admits she initially wasn’t sure what she could offer runners much faster than her. But early in the New York build, she ran with Obiri several days a week; as the workouts got faster, she paced her from a bike.

Thweatt quickly learned the role of a coach is more than just explaining and monitoring workouts and more about sharing experiences, reducing stressors, instilling confidence, visualizing race-day situations, keeping athletes focused on the process, and making sure they run easy enough on their easy days—all key elements of marathon training.

The runners are doing the work in training, but a coach is the glue that brings it all together, Thweatt says, and that’s true for any level of runner.

Kiprop says he has relied on the experience of his coaches and teammates during this first marathon build, so much so that he believes his entry into racing 26.2 miles might be easier than most. He heads to New York with a new level of fitness and plenty of firsthand course knowledge and pre-race logistics from Klecker, Obiri, Ford, Thweatt, and Ritzenhein, who all ran their first marathons on the five-borough course.

“At first, I didn’t know if I could handle the training for the marathon,” he says. “But with time, as you train together, you build that confidence, you build the courage to face the marathon.”

Ritzenhein signed on as the OAC’s first coach just weeks after his last pro race in early 2020, eager to build a program that would span more than a single Olympic cycle. He knew that would require patience, a supportive team atmosphere, and top-tier facilities.

Today, the OAC Global roster has 20 athletes from eight countries and operates out of its own 10,000-square-foot training center eight miles north of downtown Boulder, opened in 2024. It’s the nerve center for everything the team does: training, fueling, strength work, and communications. But it also serves as a place to develop camaraderie and team chemistry, which can help athletes thrive in a marathon training block, instead of just surviving.

“I think coming up with this facility was a genius idea,” Kiprop says. “It has everything we need. It’s nice to have your team around you here. When we’re together, it feels like family.”

The facility has two antigravity treadmills, eight Woodway treadmills, an underwater treadmill, and e-stim machines—most of which they use when there’s inclement weather and for rehab. There are treatment tables for massage therapists and physiotherapists, meeting space for sessions with coaches, dietitians, and mental strength counselors, and a lounge with a mini kitchen stocked with drinks, snacks, and supplements.

They also have a full gym with space for strength training, drills, and strides, an important part of their training, as marathon preparation is more than just running for the OAC crew. The team’s strength coaches, Jason Ross and Joslynn Peterson, have the runners do a wide range of running-specific and general strength exercises twice a week.

Most of the strength workouts focus on tissue health with longer isometrics (holding an exercise in one position as you would in a plank) at the beginning of a training cycle and then progress to increased weight and fewer reps, Ross tells Runner’s World. While each athlete has individual exercises to tackle, some of the common strength moves include weighted box step-ups, single-leg bent-knee hamstring isometric holds, trap bar deadlifts, landmine single-leg Romanian deadlifts, seated calf raises, and weighted standing calf raise isometrics.

“You cannot be complacent on that side of things,” Thweatt says. “It makes a huge difference. It’s an equal part of training. You need to make sure that everyone’s staying healthy and strong.”

Working alongside sports dietitians, each OAC marathoner has dialed in an individual fueling plan based on sweat testing and data from training. They know how many calories they burn on their long runs and hardest sessions, how much fluid and sodium they lose in their sweat, and exactly what they need to replace during a long run or hard session so they finish strong instead of fading late.

The exact details of what each runner needs are slightly different, Thweatt says, but they’re adept at consuming gels on the run and have practiced grabbing bottles off of tables, so they know how long they need to carry them and drink from them for optimal fueling.

“Fueling is one of the biggest things we drive home during training,” Thweatt says. “We’ve gone through the fueling plan in almost every training session that we do and we practice it like it’s going to be on race day. They know what’s going into their bottles on race day, so hopefully when we get to race day, it’s not even something they really have to think about because it’s what they’ve been doing for the last 12 weeks.”

While most runners prepare for marathons on a seven-day cycle, the OAC marathon group mostly used a nine-day schedule during this year’s 12-week buildup to both Boston and New York. No two weeks start or finish the same, but it’s a cycle with room for three long or hard sessions with two or three days of easier running in between—especially important while training at 5,400 feet, Thweatt says.

“The nine-day schedule just made sense because at altitude, with as hard as they’re running our harder sessions, we just need to make sure that we’re absorbing that training—not losing the recovery piece of it,” she explains.

At the peak of the New York build, the OAC runners logged 118 to 135 miles per week, depending on each runner’s preference and background. Klecker started his training early in July to boost his volume and eventually pushed his max to more than 130 miles a few times this fall. Ford and Obiri found their sweet spot around 120, and Kiprop, who previously averaged 100, settled in at about 110.

The biggest pieces of that volume were 35K (22-mile) and 40K (25-mile) long runs, including a couple of them at 8,500 feet on Magnolia Road west of Boulder. On the four 40K runs late in the block, Klecker, Ford, and Kiprop started at about 5:45 mile pace and worked down to 5:30 through 20K, then progressed to 5:20 for most of the final 20K, often closing near 5:00 pace.

Thweatt calls those long runs the bread and butter of the OAC training, but the key is balancing that volume and the harder, faster workouts with slower running on easy days.

After those key long runs, the OAC athletes typically run about six miles “super easy,” Thweatt says, which for them usually means as slow as 7:15 pace but as fast as 6:45 pace. Thweatt has been trying to make sure the athletes (especially Klecker and Obiri) run at those paces on their easy days to ensure they’re optimizing recovery.

The next day, the runners log double sessions of 10 miles in the morning and five miles in the afternoon, followed the next day by 12 miles in the morning and six miles in the afternoon. Those low-key maintenance runs give the mind and body a break, setting them up for one of their signature spicier workouts.

“So between big long runs or bigger sessions, we usually give them three easy days,” Thweatt says. “So you’re not touching those faster paces for three days, but you’re still getting that good quality time on feet and making sure the body is absorbing that last hard session before we hit it again with another one. Recovery is so important and it’s a piece not everyone likes to talk about as much because it's not as flashy as the big workout days.”

Two other staples of the team’s NYC build-up included 10- to 12-mile tempo runs and long, hard fartleks. The tempo runs usually start at 5:00 pace and get faster (Kiprop recently closed one at 4:45 pace), while a sample fartlek alternates “1K on” (2:50-2:55, or 4:35-4:40 mile pace) and “1K off” (3:10, or 5:05 mile pace).

“It’s about being uncomfortable for long periods of time and still trying to shift gears at the end to remind them what it’s going to be like in the marathon,” Thweatt says. “We’re trying to mirror the surges of a marathon in our workouts.”

In the final weeks, the runners also did several VO2 max sessions on the track, including two sets of 1600, 1200, 800, and 400 meters at about 5K pace, which for the OAC’s men comes out to 4:20, 3:12, 2:06, and 1:02, with the second set slightly quicker.

That kind of work has been a big change for Ford, but it has paid off.

“I was somebody that would try to approach marathon training by running at marathon pace and get really comfortable with that. But I think that only works to a certain extent,” says Ford, who just turned 29. “When I was running 2:08 to 2:09, I’d kind of be off of the pack running my own race. Now I am able to stay with the front pack and compete better.”

Unlike Chicago, Berlin, London, or Valencia, which involve mostly flat courses you can run at an even pace, the New York City Marathon is on a rolling course and pace surges play a big role in how the race plays out, Thweatt says.

Ritzenhein and Thweatt believe runners aiming for success in New York have to be able to tap into quicker-cadence running on a moment’s notice to match the terrain and competitive pickups. For example, while runners will do much of the first 16 miles at an even pace, it’s not uncommon for the lead packs to get split apart by frontrunners ratcheting up the pace (often sub-4:25 for men and sub-5:15 for women) on the 3.5-mile rolling, slightly uphill section along First Avenue on the way to the Bronx.

“Those fast track sessions in the middle to the end of a build allow us to spike the system so you can have that speed in the well for the moments you need to shift gears in a race,” Thweatt says. “With the marathon, especially with where the event is at right now with the depth and fast times, you have to touch that speed in training if you want to be competitive in the race. You can increase your volume and do longer workout sessions, but you can’t just do everything at threshold or marathon pace. It’s really important to keep that system firing and to keep it sharp so you have that speed when you need it.”

Ford credits the faster workouts for lowering his half marathon PR by 71 seconds in January (59:48) and his marathon PR by more than two minutes in Boston. He recently ran a 25K version of the 1K on/1K off fartlek, clocking a 1:03 half marathon in the middle of it.

“The reality is you’ll spend time running slower than marathon pace and you’ll spend time running faster [in New York],” he says. “Now that I’ve kind of reached this new level with the faster training with these guys, the approach is more like, ‘Let’s go to New York and try to compete with that front group.’”

Brian Metzler is a Boulder, Colorado, writer and editor whose work has appeared in Runner’s World, Sports Illustrated, ESPN, Outside, Trail Runner, The Chicago Tribune, and Red Bulletin. He’s a former walk-on college middle-distance runner who has transitioned to trail running and pack burro racing in Colorado.

#8850. At 83, Triathlete Bob Plant Isn’t Retiring—He’s Just Reloading

Sign up below to receive our newest workout routines, recipes, news stories, and offers from our partners

With the right plan and the right discipline, you can get seriously shredded in just 28 days.

At age 62, "Big Bill" shares his wisdom to dominate one of the ultimate strength marks.

Follow these fit women we're crushing on for inspiration, workout ideas, and motivation.

Bob Plant had never worried about an Ironman cutoff.

He had been to Kona before. Plenty of times, actually. This year marked his 10th start at the 2026 Ironman World Championship, and more than four decades of endurance competition had given him a good understanding of what his 83-year-old body could handle.

Kona reminded him that experience doesn’t grant immunity to a bad day.

Plant began having severe cramps in his quads and hamstrings during the bike portion of the race. He believes insufficient sodium was the primary reason, and mechanical issues compounded the problem when his chain repeatedly came loose. Each stop cost his precious time, but he didn’t realize how much until he finally reached the second transition and received news he’s never heard during an Ironman.

He had missed the bike cutoff by three minutes. His day was over.

For a triathlon Hall of Famer with seven Kona-age-group podium finishes, and 20 USA Triathlon national titles, a DNF could provide reason for second-guessing himself. But that isn’t how he’s wired.

“I just turn the page,” Plant told Muscle & Fitness. “I’ve learned something, and I’m ready to get going again.”

There wasn’t any self-pity attached to his responses around the end result. Plant believes he prepared the same way he had for his prior trips to Hawaii, only this time the clock won.

“Stuff happens like that,” he said. “You have to accept it and learn from the experience.”

That mindset helps explain as much about Plant’s athletic longevity as any training program could. He still wants to improve and remains competitive enough to care about his performance, but the decades of knowledge have taught him that surviving in the game requires knowing when to push, when to recover, and when yesterday needs to simply remain yesterday.

Plant considers himself a “minimalist trainer,” which sounds contradictory for someone who decides to line up for an Ironman.

Plant says even his friends are surprised by how much he can accomplish without the training volume you come to expect from any endurance competition. But the objective stopped being proving how much work he could put into training a long time ago.

A typical week now includes two workouts for each triathlon discipline. That’s swimming, cycling, and running. Perhaps the most important day in this routine is the one where he does absolutely nothing.

“I take one day completely off, whether I need it or not,” Plant said. “Because if I don’t take that day off, two days later, I wish I did.

For Plant, aging doesn’t necessarily mean that he’s forgotten how to work hard. It’s about knowing what the bill is that comes afterward.

“The biggest difference is you need more recovery time,” he said. “You might be able to do similar physical things that you did 10 years ago, but you’re going to need more than one day to recover. You’re probably going to need two or three days to recover.”

It’s that reality that has shaped how he thinks about training. Plant no longer does speed work because the potential injury risk and added stress aren’t worth any potential gains. Most of his work now places a priority on endurance while staying within limits he has learned over a lifetime of experience.

The discipline is knowing those limits without using age as an excuse to avoid doing anything difficult. Plant’s philosophy is listening to his body closely, so it never has to scream for his attention. Recovery isn’t lost training time. It’s when the previous session becomes useful.

“That’s when you get strong—is when you rest,” he said. “You have to repair your body and give it a chance to benefit from your hard workouts.”

Kona has only reinforced that there are other variables to manage. Plant had never missed a cutoff before. He had completed enough races on the island to believe he understood what the conditions required.

He doesn’t view that as evidence that it’s time to stop. It’s another piece of information for an athlete who still views himself as a work in progress.

For everything Plant has learned about endurance, there is one part of his current fitness that does bother him some.

Before the pandemic, strength training was a consistent fixture in Plant’s routine. He would get into the gym up to three times a week, sometimes getting a lift in right after a run. When that routine disappeared as gyms closed during covid, it never fully returned.

Plant said he could see and feel the difference.

“I think I’ve lost about–maybe just age as well–but a good seven pounds of muscle mass because I’ve not been in the gym much,” he said.

The number matters less to him than what also left with that muscle loss. Plant notices less power in his legs than he had five years ago. He still goes through his core work, stretches, and trains at home. It just can’t consistently replicate what resistance training once provided. He did acknowledge that he intends on lifting again during the winter.

Returning to strength work isn’t about hitting his max anymore or even seeing how much weight he can move. It’s about preserving what allows him to continue doing the activities he enjoys.

Plant doesn’t spend his days recovering at home in between training sessions. He still works full-time as a dentist, a career he has been in for 55 years.

Four days a week can mean arriving at the office around 7 in the morning and remaining there until after 5 p.m. On many of those evenings, he heads home to train. As he sees it, the relationship between work and fitness is mutually beneficial.

A demanding career does limit the amount of time he can dedicate to training, but Plant believes this helps protect him from overtraining. In return, his fitness gives him the physical and mental stamina to handle days in which his patients expect his complete attention regardless of how he feels.

“You just can’t say, ‘Oh, I’m going to do an average job today,’” Plant joked.

With a full day of work, there is always a reason to skip working out afterward. Like most people, Plant knows what happens once someone gets home, sits in their favorite chair, and starts negotiating with themselves about pushing their workout to another day.

He also knows what happened to him when one form of training disappeared from his own routine. The loss of strength after getting away from the gym has served as a personal reminder that physical capability isn’t something the body promises to preserve indefinitely.

“You stop doing something that you’ve been doing for a while, and you can tell the difference,” Plant said. “No doubt about it.”

Plant doesn’t expect everyone who hears his story to sign up for an Ironman. In fact, he encourages people to walk, run a 5k, or begin lifting weights. Simply find something you enjoy enough to continue doing it.

“Whether you’re walking or you’re doing some activity, just get out there and get your body moving,” he said.

He has seen people around him take versions of that message and make it their own. Someone will start exercising or complete a race and will tell Plant what they accomplished. It’s those moments that seem to matter more to him than his own results because they confirm that his example can open a door without requiring anyone to follow him through 140.6 miles.

“If I can do it at my age, surely you can do something,” Plant said. “I just encourage them to somehow look at the possibilities.”

The physical benefits are obvious, but Plant believes movement gives him something just as valuable psychologically. Training has taught him that he can tolerate discomfort, overcome difficult situations, and keep going when something doesn’t go according to plan.

“It gives you confidence,” Plant said. “You can handle an Ironman or whatever, you can handle other things in your life that may have seemed big before, but now they’re not.”

Plant would have loved to finish in Kona. He believed he could have continued if he had been allowed through transition, but the cutoff didn’t care about what potential outcomes might have been. Three minutes ended his day.

Plant accepted it. He learned what he could from his cramps, the mechanical issues, and a cutoff he had never previously needed to think about.

Then he did what more than four decades in endurance sports have taught him to do.

“I’ll continue as long as I can,” he said. “As long as it’s fun.”

Goal: Build lower-body strength, core stability, and aerobic capacity without turning every session into a maximal effort.

Time: 35–40 minutes Equipment: Dumbbells or kettlebells, bench or box, cardio machine or open space

Plant repeatedly emphasized listening to the body and giving it enough time to handle the work. The warmup should make you feel better than when you started, not tired.

Plant believes getting away from regular weight training contributed to a noticeable loss of muscle and leg power, which is why he plans to make resistance training a priority again. “If you don’t have strong legs, that’s the key to life, isn’t it?” he said.

Choose a bike, rower, treadmill, elliptical, or brisk outdoor walk.

#8849. Less Cars, More Money: My Visit to the City of the Future

In my role as Mr. Money Mustache, I do my best to be your one-stop-shop for Lifestyle Guru ideas. So over the years we’ve covered not just the Money side of life, but also the even more important stuff like health and fitness and the psychology of better, happier living.

But there’s one single area of life where all of these factors come together with an almost Nuclear Fusion level of synergy and effectiveness. And because of that, if I could have one single wish in the world, this is what I would wish for. It’s a change so massive that it would make every person on the planet better off and fix most of our problems in one grand sweep. And it’s probably not what you’d expect:

That we immediately switch to building our cities and countries around people, instead of cars.

(and then fix all of our existing ones too, so that our entire world is built around person-friendly living.)

The benefits of this are way bigger than almost anyone can imagine. We’re not just talking about eliminating a bit of pollution or a few traffic jams or car crashes. No. This is about far richer, healthier, and most importantly more fun living for everyone.

To put even conservative numbers to this, we’re talking about a life boost of over $20,000 per person per year, which compounds into well over two million dollars per adult lifetime.

On a nationwide scale, this would boost the wealth of the United States by about seven trillion dollars per year, which would compound into about 770 trillion over the next five decades.

Which happens to be more than the current total amount of human wealth on the entire planet.

You will have a house that is both cheaper and more beautiful and spacious. Your body and brain will be healthier and stronger and sexier and cost a lot less time and healthcare dollars to maintain.

And all of our wallets and investment accounts, both public and private will be absolutely overflowing with surplus income, reduced expenses, and fuel an investment and prosperity boom like the world has never seen.

“Isn’t city planning just a stuffy thing that your city council does in the background while we’re all off living our lives?”

Well, yes it is right now. And that’s the whole problem: cities are built by people whose primary job is to maintain the status quo and prevent disruptions. And those committes are elected and encouraged by crusty old companies and organizations, and plain old grumpy neighbors who just don’t have the vision to see what they are missing.

I’m convinced that if everyone could see through the smoggy haze of the status quo, we would all agree that this idea of a radical change is not only the best idea, but the only reasonable idea to even consider.

So our job is to learn and explain just how big and how easy this is. And what it boils down to is pretty damned simple.

So for the same amount of space you can have an entire pretty nice two bedroom apartment, or you can have just enough space for two (small) cars to park and pull out. But it gets even crazier than this. Check out this random intersection here in my own city:

WHAT?! So every time you have two big car roads intersect, which happens hundreds of times in every big city, you are wasting enough space to build a luxurious, resort-like living area with about one hundred two-bedroom apartments and still have room for a pool, a dog park, a grocery store, a couple of restaurants, and so on.

This is just the beginning of the insanity, because I have only shown you two parking spaces and one intersection. The reality is that our entire cities are made almost entirely of stupid, expensive wasted space like this.

And the problem is so extreme that the only reason we think we need cars to get around, is because we have wasted most of our space on accommodating cars, which spread everything out so far (and made everything so loud and dangerous) that nobody feels like walking or biking!

Whenever you propose any great new idea, you’ll always get a bunch of smartasses who like to complain and resist change, without even bothering to think it through.

“But how are we going to keep driving our cars just as much as we do now?”

Which is ridiculous – because the whole point is that as soon as you cut out all the huge wasted spaces we create to accommodate cars, you are suddenly FREE from needing cars so much!

Instead, you can just weave a brand new city, with a bunch of variations of this beautiful resort which also include offices, grocery stores, climbing gyms and every other amenity.

And yes, you’d still have some roads between them, but they would be mostly for deliveries, emergency vehicles and people who need mobility assistance.

I hope you’re not going to make me ride the bus?

I am all for public transit in theory, but to be honest I don’t usually have the patience for it. I don’t do lineups, and I don’t like to stand around waiting passively for my transportation to arrive – when it’s time to go somewhere, I just want to go, and go now, and get there fast. So my own personal choice is to take a bike for short distances (under 2 miles) or an e-bike for larger ones (up to about 15 miles).

Although this is often news to car drivers, bikes are much faster than cars for urban transport, plus they give me exercise and thrill, which is way better than being stuck at the red light with the cars.

If you take this already-superior method of urban transport and cut out the 90% of the land that we waste on accommodating the inferior cars, then you end up with a revolution: everybody gets where they are going ten times faster, at much lower cost, and has much more fun doing it.

And sure, there will also be light rail and faster buses. And sure, you can still hop in an Uber or even bring your own car into a city like this.But the point is that it will just happen much much less often.

Okay I’m convinced, but how can we actually accomplish this?

Mr. Money Mustache can talk a big game with all these fancy words and pictures, but the truth is that I’m way too impatient to put up with all the bureaucracy and complaints that arise when you try to actually change a city. I’ve been doing my best here in Longmont, and I have gotten just about nowhere. We’re still just stacking on more and more layers of ridiculous car shit where I live.

Thankfully, other people are much more patient and effective than I am at affecting change, and one group has made such incredible progress that you can now go LIVE in their first creation: a 1000-person car-free neighborhood called Culdesac Tempe. And as I write this, I am staying in a hotel right nearby, having spent the past two days touring and visiting and interviewing the founders*.

While we were at it, my Phoenix-area-house-fixing friend Tracy Royce and I also hosted a meetup for an enthusiastic group of our readers/viewers right there in Culdesac’s emerging central plaza.

Culdesac is Awesome and Could Change Everything

If you only look at the financial spreadsheet, you would think this first Culdesac project is just going to be a highly profitable 1000-person cluster of apartment buildings, spread out across 17 acres of land. And while financial sustainability is indeed a key reason why this model will succeed, the money is the least exciting part.

When you look at these pictures compared to a normal housing complex, the main thing you will notice is that all the space that would normally be wasted on parking lots, is instead used for beautiful walking and gathering areas.

The next big upgrade is that they mixed in the amenities for daily life right into the neighborhood, rather than forcing all the future residents to get into their cars to drive out to find them:

I was also impressed with just the feel of walking the Mediterranean-vibed spaces between the buildings, even at this early stage when everything is still under construction.

Due to the hot desert climate of the region, everything is built around providing shade, breeze, and reflecting heat during the summer, while also maximizing the joyful fact that there is no winter there (the coldest month of the year still has an average daily high of 65F/18C, which means palm trees, leafy gardens and fruits and flowers forever.)

With a setup like this, and 999 new neighbors to meet, I would rarely feel the need to leave the place. Which really cuts down on my desire to use a car. But on top of that, Culdesac has strategically placed itself in Tempe, a city right in the center of the Phoenix metro area, within walking distance of the main university and right on a light rail stop which allows you to reach almost everything (including the airport) for FREE, since an annual pass to the transit system is included with your rent.

But of course, you can also get around on foot, bike, e-bike, scooter, or hop into one of Culdesac’s fleet of rideshare electric cars for a trip to the mountains or whatever else you might want to do that’s outside of bike and transit range.

It’s insane. In fact it’s so good that I am going to attempt to move there myself at the end of 2023, enjoying my first escape from Colorado winter and celebrating the fact that my boy will be a legal adult at that time.

But even this is just a pilot project because Culdesac has much bigger plans.

From my conversations with the founders, I think they want to do this:

So How Can We Benefit From This, and Support it?

This whole change is exciting, and it is immense.

Understanding these ideas around city planning is the economic and social equivalent to being a doctor, and finding a 35-year-old patient in a hospital who is suffering from every chronic disease, but then discovering that they have been following a diet of Coke and Donuts for their whole lives and never been out on a walk, once.

Good point Stephanie – I believe that part is coming soon, as the first batch of apartments open up and are ready for rent (right now you are only signing up for the waiting list rather than an actual apartment).

Since I was there and asked the same question in person, the answer is basically “market rate” – in other words, when a new apartment goes up for rent, the builders typically conduct a price survey of what would be a competitive price at that moment, and then they start advertising at that price.

Just like any other supply and demand sensitive thing, these prices will then fluctuate based on the demand level until you lock it in with a lease. During my tour, it was a hot time for rentals in prosperous Tempe so the rent was around $2.50 per square foot per month, or a little under $2k for a large 1-bedroom apartment.

Note that at Culdesac you get a few extra perks included in that rent: internet access that works across the whole 17 acre campus, gym, pool, and unlimited transit pass along with credits for bike and carshare as well.

Francesco, you have it great in Rome. I live in Montreal, and cars are a needless, dangerous polluting bother. Our metro (subway) is very reliable, frequent and fast and there are wonderful bike paths that go almost everywhere. I personally prefer skateboarding to and from metro stations since it’s easy to just carry the skateboard on the train and pop back on it afterwards.

That said, there is a huge massive disgusting traffic jam covering the whole city all the time and it stinks and is painful if you ever have to drive for any reason, but more and more streets are being pedestrianized and we can dream about ditching cars altogether. Whenever you can ditch cars do so, it’s better for you and the planet.

I am originally from Phoenix and one of the reasons I left 10 years ago is because I really disliked the car-centric culture and the soullessness of the vast Phoenix suburbs. I lived abroad first and then moved to an East Coast city and haven’t had a car in 10 years (and I love it!). I miss my family and friends there but ultimately prioritized my health and lifestyle by moving to a location that wasn’t car-dependent.

My parents still live in the Phoenix area and their health is deteriorating to the point where driving isn’t feasible anymore. They are basically stuck at home or dependent on friends driving them around. Culdesac could be a game changer for them. I’m actually visiting them later this month and hope I can convince them to take a tour. This type of intentional urban planning can also be really beneficial for people with disabilities or who aren’t (for whatever reason) able to drive anymore, beyond just personal preference. Plus the social, mental, physical, and financial benefits are immense!

I wanted to add — MMM, I recommend you reconsider your stance on public transit! I think your current perspective is based on the limitations of most North American public transit systems. You mention not liking the lineups and waiting, but with proper investment, this would be minimal, and mass transit would be quite efficient (and currently is in many parts of the world!). I absolute agree with your stance on bikes, but it should be a “both and,” not an “either or!” If we’re envisioning the world with the urban planning we want to see, let’s imagine having boundless multimodal options, like taking the subway across the entire city and then grabbing a bike share for the last mile. Advocating for cities to invest both in bike lines and increased mass transit is beneficial to all in the long-term and they both work in tandem to reduce expensive and isolating car-centric culture.

An ideal transit system would be: – walk a maximum of 1-2 blocks from your start, and the same at the destination. – wait no more than 5 minutes, out of severe weather (covered shelter) – few or no transfers, minimum wait time at transfer points – a good app to help with complex route planning.

I have the first and last of these. Bus frequency on my closest routes is 15 minutes, ok but not great. I can get to some places with no or one easy transfer, but many places in my city have awful routes. [Over an hour for what would be a 12 minute car ride.] It’s getting better, but very slowly.

As far as apps go, I use and like Transit.

Serious question, where do the people who work in the shops and stores live. I can imagine this community is not cheap. I am thinking of Prospect in Longmont. Beautiful, walkable, but crazy expensive. Can the barista who works in the coffee shop afford to live there? Your trash gets hauled away, and the sewage disappears. You get to live in a rich nice community. Good for you, same for them.

Great question Doug. Culdesac is definitely going to be very expensive and exclusive, and yes in a bad way. The people who work in it’s stores will live in other, worse neighborhoods. However, they will be able to take the light rail (or bike) in to work, and hopefully it will inspire more new neighborhoods in more places. The rich have the disposable income to try new things, unfortunately the poor have to largely take what they can get until they save enough to escape. So I wish it was more inclusive, but just look at it as a start.

Looking on their website, studios are available from $1340/month. Assuming a barista makes $15/hr, that’s $2395/month after taxes if they work full time. That’s a fair chunk of their income in rent, but not impossible. They could also share a two bedroom for $1080 each. Given their internet is paid for, their gym is paid for, and there’s no car payment (assuming they to carless), that leaves $1055 a month free for other bills and groceries. I love the idea of car-free communities, but don’t see them going mainstream for a number of reasons that have nothing to do with planning commissions and city councils (sat on both for about a decade and, believe or not, we really do want walkable communities). Still, we can dream!

Years ago, I took a permaculture course, and found all of the urban planning bits the most interesting… it’s been awhile, but I remember reading some of the book “A Pattern Language”, and thinking that the author was on to something. Homes and communities that have been built with inate human nature in mind (intentionally or not) feel the best and are the healthiest. That’s why you get a certain “this feels good” feeling n the oldest human cities and villages and quite the opposite when in expansive car dominated grid pattern American cities. I just called them. So the main ‘street’ (In this picture – looks like it is called ‘Primary Paseo’: https://www.mrmoneymustache.com/wp-content/uploads/2023/04/culdesac-architecture.jpg), was deliberately planned to accommodate emergency vehicles, including firetrucks.

For some of the smaller sidestreets/paseos, if an ambulance is unable to fit, they would park as close as possible (either inside or outside of the community) and then use standard methods (rolling stretcher, etc..) to bring patients back to the vehicle. The major concern I have with ANYTHING in Arizona is WATER! Where does their water come from and how will they be able to provide water into the future? Arizona already has big supply problems and recklessly continues to build out in the desert. This issue will become worse and already has forced some people to leave their desert houses. It will result in ghost communities. Who can say it won’t happen in the city of Phoenix, too?

Mr. Money Mustache April 8, 2023, 6:43 pm

Believe it or not, this is not a big problem in Phoenix and most other big desert cities. They have plenty of water for domestic use. It’s agriculture that uses the lion’s share of fresh water – about 80% of it in the Western US. Then our other industrial uses, then our houses are down near the bottom.

One major improvement in places like Phoenix and Las Vegas versus the rest of the country is that they have managed to mostly eliminate suburban lawns. A single patch of lawn watered in the desert will use more than an entire household, so as soon as you remove that you have made the whole city more sustainable.

Alas, here in the Denver area the lawn with the big sprinkler system still seems to be in style, despite the fact that our summer climate very closely resembles a real desert. The grass will die within a week or two if you leave it unwatered, which I think would be a great idea in most cases. There’s lots of cool stuff you can do with river rocks and native flowers and Yucca plants that takes almost no water to sustain!

Very accurate, MMM! I’ve got a good friend who works for whatever they call the “water” department of the city of Mesa (right next to Tempe), and whenever I bring up the metro Phoenix water supply issue, he basically says “we’ll be fine, but things will have to change with respect to agriculture in the southwest and lawns/golf courses”.

I worried about it for years, but a bit of research and several articles in the NYT helped calm me down. Here’s one: https://www.nytimes.com/interactive/2023/05/22/climate/colorado-river-water.html .

TLDR: We’re going to have to continue to evolve what we raise/grow/eat to balance the demands on our planet, especially considering climate change (to the surprise of practically nobody reading MMM)

Please forgive me for giving vent to one of my pet peeves.

It’s FEWER cars, not LESS. Fewer is used when referring to things (people, cars, buildings, bottles of beer) that can be counted separately. Less is used when referring to things (sugar, coffee) that come in bulk.

Of course, your usage is rapidly becoming the standard now, which drives irascible old English majors like me nuts. But that’s how language works, which is why we no longer talk like Chaucer or Shakespeare.

#8847. Five Glute Moves for Making Massive Lower-Body Gains

Sign up below to receive our newest workout routines, recipes, news stories, and offers from our partners

With the right plan and the right discipline, you can get seriously shredded in just 28 days.

At age 62, "Big Bill" shares his wisdom to dominate one of the ultimate strength marks.

Follow these fit women we're crushing on for inspiration, workout ideas, and motivation.

Australian weightlifter, personal trainer, and busy mom Stephanie Sanzo is known for staying in shape while balancing family life, so when it comes to firming her glutes, the buff beauty finds success in simple workouts that require maximum effort. Recently, Sanzo shared her booty building process on social media, so that others can work towards their own glute gains.

The workout, shared with Sanzo’s 3.3 million followers on Instagram, had viewers understandably inspired to replicate her reps. “Steph proving that muscles don’t take away from femininity,” wrote one user. “The best,” added another,” and “Saved” wrote yet another fired-up follower. Here’s how to try it for yourself.

Understanding that muscles grow by adapting to progressive overload, Sanzo uses her rep scheme to aim for hypertrophy, starting out with a taxing drop tri-set that sets the bar for what’s to come. The standing hip thrusts, targeting the glutes and hamstrings include 35 reps across three sets.

From then on, each exercise takes in three sets with a short rest allowed, and that’s just as well, because the reps rise all the way to 60 by the time Sanzo reaches the RDL finisher. Note: If your gym doesn’t have a standing hip thrust machine, the coach suggests standing cable pull throughs as a similar alternative.

Second-up is the traditional barbell hip thrust, building glute strength and mass with the support of a bench for her upper body and hitting a straight line at the top of the lift. The third move is the rack supported dumbbell Bulgarian split squat. The purpose of using the rack, or anything else available for support, is that this helps to isolate the lower body and require less muscle recruitment from the upper body for balance. Of course, Sanzo characteristically ups the intensity by adding dumbbells, hammering the glutes, pelvis, and hamstrings as she goes.

Moving back to the machines for her fourth exercise, Sanzo sits down on the hip abduction machine to work the outer hips in a way that is difficult to achieve with free weights. Stronger hip abductors improve stability in the core and pelvis, aiding mobility and making other glute exercises easier to execute. Also, adding mass to the outer hip region muscles, like the gluteus medius, will help to add some roundness to your rear.

For her finisher, Sanzo leaves it all in the gym with three heavy sets of bench supported dumbbell Romanian Deadlifts. Keeping her legs straight, the fit female contracts her glutes and core as she crushes each lift, blasting her glutes and hamstrings before hitting a well-earned shower.

If you’re chasing a simple glute focused workout that will leave you feeling the burn, this one’s for you.
